subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF SELECT STANDING COMMITTEE

speechtext: Mr. F. W. TURNBULL (Regina) moved concurrence in the second report of the select standing committee on industrial and international relations.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF SELECT STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Would my hon. friend mind informing us just what the recommendations are?

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF SELECT STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: The report of the committee appears in the votes and proceedings. Briefly, the committee did not agree that there was any money spent in Canada on war, that the expenditures of the Department of National Defence were not war expenditures. Secondly, the committee was of the opinion that professorships and scholarships were not practicable to establish, first by reason of the expense entailed, and second by reason of difficulties of legislative jurisdiction as between the provinces and the Dominion. The third recommendation of the committee is that books on inter-imperial and international relations should be added from time to time to the library in the Department of External Affairs, and the fourth recommendation commends the League of Nations Society in Canada to members of parliament and to the people of Canada generally, and suggests continued support thereof.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF SELECT STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I do not agree, Mr. Speaker, with the first two recommendations of the committee.
I do not agree with the statement of the committee that expenditure for national defence and cadet training is not money spent on war, because I think that defence when there is no war is really war in an inactive period or a native war. I do not agree with those two recommendations, and I shall say no more about them.
The committee also is of the opinion that scholarships and chairs on international relationships are not feasible partly because of the expense necessary for the establishment of the chairs, and partly by reason of the question of legislative jurisdiction as between the provinces and the Dominion. If scholarships and a chair in even one university would do anything at all to prevent war, I think we could very well afford it because we have spent huge sums and are still spending very considerable sums on defence. I do not agree that we cannot afford to spend the money necessary for the establishment of international professorships and scholarships. The other reason against such establishment given by the committee is the constitutional difficulties in the way. So long as we have a Royal Military college the money for which is voted by this parliament, the college being under federal jurisdiction, so long as the federal parliament is voting sums of money for technical education and cadet training or military education in schools, I do not and will not agree that there is a constitutional difficulty. Besides that we have the Minister of Justice in the late government (Mr. Lapointe) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) in this government, as well as eminent professors of international law at McGill and Toronto universities, all saying that the constitutional difficulty can be got around. I think, therefore, we can conclude that whatever the reason is that we do not go forward with scholarships at the moment, it is not the reason given in the report. My opinion is that we are not interested enough, and the moment that we are, we shall find ways of spending money for scholarships on international relations.
The third recommendation of the committee deals with the extension of the library of the Department of External Affairs and the making of that library available to research students. That recommendation is an admirable one, and I think it may be the beginning of a sort of summer school to which students ol this particular subject can come and study. It may be that in the near future they may have the help of a librarian or professor, or someone who knows the work there.

Industrial Relations Report

The fourth clause of the committee's report is a pious wish for the success of the League of Nations Society in Canada. That is possibly better than nothing, but I am not so sure that it is much better than nothing, though I agree with it as far as it goes. That is all I care to say at the moment.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN THIRD REPORT OF SELECT STANDING COMMITTEE

speechtext:
Hon. J. D. CHAPLIN (Lincoln) moved for concurrence in the third and final report of the select standing committee on railways and shipping, owned, operated and controlled by the government.
Mr. JOHN T. HACKETT (Stanstead): Mr. Speaker, before this document is relegated to the limbo of things futile I should like to say a few words about its subject matter. The Canadian government is engaged in a rather large way in the business of transportation both on land and sea. On land the Canadian National Railways own and operate 23,668 miles of first track steam mileage in which are included 3,342 miles of eastern lines. Eastern lines are defined by the Maritime Freight Rates Act of 1927 as those lines lying east of Levis, Quebec. From July 1, 1927, the rates on those lines have been reduced by 20 per cent, and the government has made up the difference. The Canadian National Railways also operate 187 miles of electric lines. At sea they operate a coastal service on the Pacific coast of six vessels; three of them in the triangular service between Vancouver, Victoria and Seattle; two other ships are in the island service; two ships, the Dalhousie City and the Northumberland, on lake Ontario are operated under the name of the Niagara, St. Catharines and Toronto Navigation Company. They operate also two vessels plying between Chicago and Depot Harbour, a car ferry between Chicago and Milwaukee, a car ferry between Piotou and Mulgrave and two car ferries between Borden and Tormentine. The Canadian Government Merchant Marine owns a fleet of thirty vessels; a few years ago there were 60 vessels. The total tonnage at the present time is 239,170 tons. The Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships Limited operate twelve ships between Canada and the West Indies with a total tonnage of 60,592 tons. The government owns and will soon operate the Hudson Bay railway with a mileage of 510 miles.
My purpose in reciting these facts is to acquaint the country with this great enterprise and its cost during the last twelve years. The amounts which I shall give are disbursements which have been made either in cash or credit by the Canadian people since April 1, 1919. I may say that at the moment those disbursements amount to $1,663,675,517.61. I have before me the details of this sum. In cash we advanced to the Canadian National Railways between April 1, 1919, and March 31, 1923,
$389,743,789.34. From April 1, 1923, to December 31, 1930, we advanced $57,482,652.91, making a total of $447,226,442.25. We guaranteed the bonds of the Canadian National Railways to the extent of $569,609,027. Included in that amount are $77,000,000 of retirements. In addition to this new capital we have secured to the railways $216,207,141.67, by guaranteeing the interest in perpetuity on the Grand Trunk railway guaranteed and debenture stock. Moreover we have guaranteed as to capital and interest Canadian National Railways debenture stock, of which there now remains outstanding $30,559,114. There has also been purchased equipment, for which equipment trust notes have been issued and remain outstanding to the amount of $94,680,000. These notes are not guaranteed, but the conditions under which they were issued make the country entirely responsible for them if the railways continue to operate. Under the Maritime Freight Rates Act there has been paid to the Canadian National Railways $7,897,360. The requirements of the Canadian National Railways for deficits, acquisitions and betterments for the present, year are $120,000,000. I wish to say on that score that the amount estimated was $104,000,000. It was admitted, however, by the railway management when before the committee that although the estimates were prepared in April they were already $13,000,000 short. I think in view of present conditions it is a conservative estimate to place those requirements for the present year at $120,000,000. Furthermore we are pledged for $48,250,000 after this year's program of construction is completed; that includes branch lines, terminals at Montreal and the hotels at Saskatoon, Jasper and Vancouver.
With regard to the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, we were told that if this business were wound up to-day it would have cost the people of Canada $81,222,769.90, without allowing anything for interest. The 'deficit on the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, if we assume that it will be this year what it was last year, will be $588,500. We invested in the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamship Company $9,804,715. The deficit on that service last year was $523,136.98, and it is fair to assume it will not be less this year. This makes no allowance for interest.
Our investment in the Hudson Bay railway is something like $45,000,000, but since 1919 we have put into the Hudson Bay railway and terminals $31,756,417.

If the hon. gentleman
were listening he would not ask the question. There also has been spent on the ear ferry at Prince Edward Island $2,500,000. Under the Maritime Freight Rates Act there has also been paid $2,922,891 to railways other than the Canadian National. These different items make a total of $166,367,551,761.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not think these figures can be controverted; in fact I have culled them from the records of the company and of the department. But it is one thing to hear and quite another thing to comprehend them. We all know that there comes a time when language utterly fails us. We know that the symbols of speech when used to express either facts or phenomena that are beyond our personal experience do not convey very much to us. It will be recalled that after the Franco-Prussian war when France, the richest nation of Europe, was condemned to pay to Germany $1,000,000,000, or 5,000,000,000 francs, it did not mean very much to anybody, because 5,000,000,000, or even 1,000,000 francs, was so far beyond the experience of the, ordinary individual that it conveyed no definite idea. But when the gold began to move from France to Germany in carload lots, then the people understood what it meant, a carload was something within their grasp; then they realized the enormous indemnity which their country was called upon to pay.
This is the difficulty which confronts one when he attempts to explain something that is beyond the experience of his audience; it is the difficulty of the schoolmaster; it is particularly the difficulty of the clergyman. Who has not listened to laboured efforts on the part of clergymen attempting to describe the celestial sphere, or the beatific vision, or the deity or something else that has never been heard or seen? I recall once hearing a clergyman say in an attempt to describe the endlessness of eternity, that if a mountain which rose high above the plain were worn down level with it by the brush of a swallow's wing which passed over it once in a thousand years, then eternity would only have begun.
I think the Canadian people find themselves in a somewhat similar difficulty when attempting to comprehend, to understand, to grasp the full meaning of the indebtedness that has been placed upon them in the last twelve years. When one is confronted by this difficulty he resorts to indirect and possibly to inadequate means; he resorts to comparison, to anything that may illustrate, even indirectly, the point which he is trying to make. With that end in view may I point

out that in the first forty years of confederation we added to our national debt at the rate of only $7,000,000 a year, so that on the fortieth anniversary of confederation we had added but $280,000,000 odd to the original obligation. Yet during the last thirteen years we have added to our national liabilities something like $130,000,000 a year for the purposes of transportation alone. For the last year of which the record has been completed the total expenditure of the government of Canada for all services was but $383,000,000, including something over $25,000,000 of capital expenditures. Yet the Canadian National Railways alone-and I may say to the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer) that a few moments ago I was not speaking exclusively of the Canadian National Railways, I was speaking of the venture in transportation on land and on sea, of the Canadian government-yet the Canadian National Railways alone spent last year, not $380,000,000 which the nation spent to carry on its work, but $421,071,409. The total pay-roll of the government of Canada in all services was but $90,808,425.71, whereas the Canadian National Railways paid out in Canada alone $159,675,000 for wages. The total number of employees of the Canadian government last year was 44,000, of the Canadian National Railways 100,678. The carrying charges in the form of interest on the funded debt due from the Canadian National Railways to the public at the end of this year will be $60,000,000, and in 1919 it was but an insignificant figure. On the eve of the war the total expenditure of the government reached the unprecedented figure of $144,000,000 a year. Yet the railways required from this country in new capital in 1929, $144,670,459 and $148,000,000 in 1930. I have cited these figures not for the purpose of arguing that any or all of these amounts have been improperly spent. I am attempting merely to make the point that the business of transportation as carried on by the Canadian National Railways is a far greater business in dollars and cents, in enterprise, in salary and in number of employees than is the business of administering Canada itself. And what precautions have we taken, as a people and as a parliament, that this administration be carried on as it should be? When moneys are spent by governments they are very carefully scrutinized; estimates come before the committee of the whole and sometimes hours are spent in discussing just how a few hundred dollars should be spent. Very frequently one avails himself of that opportunity to discuss how a few hundred dollars have been spent. When ways and means reso-

Railways and Shipping Report
lutions come before parliament they are debated very carefully, yet when we called into existence the Canadian National Railways the very first thing we did was to kill the watch dog. By the statute which brought the Canadian National into existence we eliminated any interference or supervision by the auditor general, who is sent into every department of government to scrutinize, to check up and to certify as to the exactitude and propriety of every cent of expenditure. Yet when it came to the Canadian National Railways; in which we have billions of dollars invested, we utterly failed to exercise the most elementary prudence.
When we created this vast corporation, which constitutes the greatest mass of property brought under centralized control in Canada, and one of the greatest masses of property subject to unified control in the world, what precautions did we take? We put it into the hands of a manager, and over that manager we put a board of directors. Who constitute that board of directors? Honest gentlemen? That is conceded. Honourable gentlemen? Oh, yes. Good railway men? I am not certain how many of them know a hay rake from a hand car. What qualifications have they for the high office which they hold? There may be some exceptions but many of them have not, either by experience, by training or by aptitude the necessary capacity or opportunity to protect the country's purse. In my humble estimation if there is one thing more futile than the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways-more futile, be it understood, for the purpose for which directors are supposed to exist, which is to direct, to control, to supervise and to safeguard the interests of the shareholders, who are the people of Canada-it is this select committee on railways and shipping which, in a few short sittings, is supposed to check up the millions of dollars annually spent and make a report on the actions of the management and the board. If it were not so tragic it would be amusing. That a people who pride themselves on their enterprise and who have taken their place in the sun should, in a matter of business, be so absolutely lacking in the elements of common sense is 'beyond comprehension.

We have gone on with this noble experiment, as it has been called
by some of its protagonists, for nearly thirteen years, and I submit that there are two or three facts which are absolutely incontrovertible. The first fact is that there is not in Canada sufficient business to maintain these railways in the state of efficiency in which they are operated at the present time. The second is that we cannot go on paying into the coffers of this company, to make up deficits, to acquire betterments and build extensions, a hundred to a hundred and fifty million dollars a year. The third is that the management has failed in the task which was allotted to it. The management was set up for what purpose? It came here to solve our railway problem. Has it done so?

Yes? Any hon. gentleman who thinks our railway problem has been solved may select for himself a place in either category, that of the innocent or the ignorant. Any man who has seen our debt increased by $1,600,000,000 in the last twelve or thirteen years; any man who has seen the dead weight imposed upon the people increased to $60,000,000 a year in the payment of interest on funded debt alone and who thinks a solution has been found does not commend himself, I submit, to the good judgment of the people of the country.
I admit that the service provided by these railways is good; I admit that the personnel, the equipment and the road bed have all been carried to a high point of efficiency. But I consider that the capital expenditures and some of the administrative charges have been injudicious, lavish and incurred without any regard to our needs or our capacity to pay. Show me a single venture in the Canadian National enterprise that has succeeded according to the rule of profit and loss. There has not been a single venture, be it the hotels, the triangular or the coastal service on the Pacific, the Canadian Government merchant marine, or the Canadian National West Indies service, that has yielded one cent of profit.
I know that my hon. friend who sits opposite, the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler), has said forsooth that public ownership of public utilities has a greater and higher purpose than that of profit: it is service, and service at cost. I ask, at what cost? An amount of $604,000,000 in cash was put into this enterprise, all with the exception of $157,000,000 after the bankruptcy, every dollar of which was used by the company; and the hon. gentleman has argued that this should not form a part of the capital of the railways.
Now what is going to be done? The management has offered this solution: it suggests that we scrap the merchant marine. I have no objection to that, it is probably unfortunate for the taxpayer that this course was not pursued some years ago. Then the suggestion is made with regard to the railway itself, that we appoint a commission to investigate the condition of transportation in Canada. I take that to mean, Mr. Speaker, that the management feels that its effort of the last eight years has been unproductive and that it is incapable of finding a solution to our problem. It means that if it means anything.
I am not sure that it was possible to find a solution in the circumstances in which the management found itself. Commissions in the past have been a haven for those who were perplexed, and have furnished fodder for pigeon holes. However, commissions, like governments, are good, bad or indifferent as the men who comprise them are competent or otherwise. If a commission of men, judiciously selected and competent, cared to undertake the solution of this problem, I daresay it might yield to their treatment. I consider that the government is better able than any commission to deal with this situation; it is more capable of dealing with it, especially from the financial point of view. There is a limit quite regardless of what may have happened in the last thirteen years to the credit of the country. It is necessary, when we decide upon the future policy of this transportation system, that we realize that our treasury is not inexhaustible. I believe that the government, with such assistance

as it can commandeer from the railways, and possibly from some outside sources, is in a better position than any other body of men to deal with this problem promptly and effectively.

What outside sources?
Mr. HAOKiETT: Riviere du Loup. But while we are dealing with this question, it seems to me that there are some aspects of it which are more urgent than others. In the first place, whatever may have been the success of the management in its administration of the properties there is one field in which it is absolutely supreme. It has outshone all its rivals in the gentle art of publicity. The Canadian National Railways have monopolized the agencies for disseminating news. They have their own publications which in no way minimize either the virtue or the achievements of those who form part of that organization.

speechtext: What is wrong with that?

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN THIRD REPORT OF SELECT STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
They control the radio service; they have a telegraph service; and they have so demeaned themselves towards the press of the country that, with a few rare exceptions, any copy which is not laudatory of the Canadian National is not good and fit copy to go to the public of Canada. I say, Mr. Speaker, that so long as this method obtains, this method of suppression which withholds news and which prevents public opinion from being formed, there hangs over the Canadian National system and over this country a peril which shortly will do it great harm. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the great public of the country should be acquainted with the Railway situation. They should be acquainted with all its details; the people whose road this is-an institution which is of the people and for the people-should be thoroughly known to the public in all of its activities.
Another aspect of the situation which in my view requires immediate attention is the curtailment of all non-productive expenditures. I am of those who believe that steam traction ultimately will come back into its own, but at the present time it is challenged as it never has been challenged before. It is challenged on land by the auto truck and by the passenger automobile. It is challenged by the ocean; the Panama canal has done much to minimize the transcontinental movement of freight. The Hudson Bay railway was built for that very purpose. It is challenged by the deep waterways, that projected system of transportation

Railways and Shipping Report
which has emerged from the realm of theoretical discussion and is rapidly becoming one of practical politics. If it becomes a reality, it must of necessity take much freight from the railways of Canada. It is even challenged from the air. Until we know what success awaits our steam roads, until we know they are going to withstand these challenges, and resist the inroads which are being made on their earnings, it behooves us to go slowly and discontinue these large capital expenditures, it behooves us to exercise some element of control. Whether this control can be exercised by appointing directors who know something about railroading, men who can give their full time to this work and who will not be selected because of some accident of political stripe or residence, men who will know something about the problems to be solved and who will be able to render useful service, or by naming some official of the government to direct and check expenditures, I know not, but it is abundantly apparent from the events of the last few months that such an element of control is needed.
I suggest that these publicly owned roads be made to pay their way and that future deficits be paid out of taxes. It is only by this means that the public will have an opportunity of becoming acquainted with these roads and knowing whether or not the benefits they confer are worth the price which they cost. We have been charging deficits to capital account and thus saddling the future with a heavy burden. The full cost of railway transport must be paid either by the classes served, by the taxpayers of the time, or, with compound interest, by posterity. To spread this cost over a long period in the name of constructive benevolence is to dull the instrument of financial criticism by which all well-ordered communities locate and analyze their financial weaknesses. Worse than that, Mr. Speaker, it is a direct invitation to posterity to indulge in that all-shattering denial- repudiation. Something should be done and done now. Every way we have turned during the last six months in an effort to curtail expenditure we have been told that we were too late. We were too late because a contract had been signed here, a sod turned there, or a statute passed here. The mocking spectre of "Too late'-' has dogged our steps for the last six months. I ask that something be done now to preclude further commitments before it is too late, not only for the roads but for Canada.

My right hon. friend brings
up the matter of geography. I think he might find that even in the province of British Columbia there are men who would be absolutely competent and well qualified to serve as members of the board. May I say quite sincerely that if I were so fortunate, or so unfortunate as to have to attend to the appointment of members of the board of the Canadian National Railways I would not make my choice with any view to provincial allotment at all. I would try to obtain five, six, or eight, or whatever the proper number may be, men qualified for the work they would have to do. I would say further that we cannot expect the members of that board to give a considerable part of their time to the work of the board for the miserable pittance of $2,000 a year. True, there may be many men in Canada who possess a great degree of public spirit and are willing to give up their time and services for the public good. As a general rule however a man will generally do what he is paid to do. I make the suggestion, even if in a measure it may be a criticism of past governments, that in the appointment of members to the board of the Canadian National Railways consideration be given only to one matter, namely qualification for the work. There should be higher salaries paid so that it may be worth while for men to give their time and attention to the work of the board. So that we would not lose the benefit of the experience of men who have attained knowledge and ability in the management of the railways, it might be well if the terms of office did not terminate at the same time. Members might be appointed for two or three years, or five years, and at intervals as some members retire from the board some experienced men would remain so as to eliminate the possibility of

Railways and Shipping Report
an entirely new board, none of the members of which would be familiar with railway practice.
That is a responsibility of the present government, and I should like to remind my hon. friend from Stanstead (Mr. Haekett) of that fact. He made one or two further criticisms, and another one which I shall leave to the last. He blamed the management, and in that connection I am not going to speak at length. I know there have been many rumours and charges about which I am going to say nothing. I believe the report of the committee might be accepted by parliament as speaking for itself. There have been charges of extravagance; something has been said about the building of hotels, and so on. If I so desired I could make comparisons, but I do not intend to enter into that phase of the discussion at all because, as I say, comparisons are odious and would lead only to discussions of no practical value. If there is extravagance I would say that it is a matter entirely within the control of the present government and the board appointed by it. If there is one statement I might make-and I do not wish my remarks to be construed as a criticism of the committee-if there is one thing in connection with which we may have gone a little farther afield than at times I thought we should go, it is that to some extent we were trying to do the work which properly belongs to the board of directors enjoying the confidence of this government.
Then my hon. friend made a further significant statement. He said that there is not enough business for the two railways. Perhaps he is right, but I wonder what inference he wishes the house to draw from that remark. When he makes that statement I think it is due to hon. members that he tell what the remedy should be. He says the railway has not been placed on its feet. I would say to him1-and this statement applies to both railways, which are in the same position, although he has seen fit to criticize one and not the other-that those railways are bound by the laws of Canada to charge certain freight and passenger rates. I believe I am stating a fact when I say that if the freight rates in Canada had been as high as they are in the United1 States the Canadian National Railways would not be registering deficits but would be showing profits. Those lower rates have been for the good of the Canadian people; we have enjoyed lower rates in Canada, although we live in a less thickly populated country than do our neighbours to the south.
I have nothing further to say except that I think my hon. friend from Stanstead did not complete his speech. From beginning to end his words have been full of criticism, and I wonder what good they will do. I do not believe his speech will have a great deal of effect in destroying the confidence of the Canadian people in their National railway system. He has made the statement that the Canadian National Railways control the press -a statement which I regard as an insult to the responsible and respectable press of this country. I do not believe his statement that the Canadian National Railways control the press is founded on fact. I do not believe however that his criticism will have any greater tangible result than had the flight of the swallow against the mountain, of which he spoke. If there is anything in my hon. friend's statement that there is not enough business for the two railway campanies, which railway does he wish to survive. If my hon. friend and the people of Quebec do not know it, I think I am speaking for the people of the province of Ontario and the members on both sides of this house from that province when I say that we have a real confidence and belief in the principle of public ownership so far as the Canadian National railways are concerned.
Mr. JEAN-FRANQOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): Mr. Speaker one day the member for Temiscouata asked the Minister of Railways:
Is the minister _ aware that the station at Riviere du Lr>np is in a deplorable condition aud entirely unsuited to the requirements of the officials compelled to remain there?
The minister answered:
The minister is aware that the station is requiring certain repairs. Plans are prepared, and it is proposed to proceed with the work of improvement.
This answer was given by Mr. Blair, the then Minister of Railways and Canals, to a question put by my predecessor, the late Mr, Gauvreau, on February 26, 1900, at page 1006 of Hansard. The station was remodelled and enlarged in 1900, and for thirty-one years there have been no repairs.
Photographs were taken and shown to hon. members on June 10, 1931. It was impossible to take photographs of the inside of the station because of the extreme darkness. That very respectable Conservative paper the Toronto Mail and Empire contained the following statement on June 11:
The photographs were taken with a view to showing proof of Mr. Pouliot's complaints. On the set filed with the clerk, he has marked out what he terms the rats' entrance to the station, the manner in which the roof is warped and the ease with which rain water can-and does, be says-flood the station cellar every time RivieTe du Loup has one of its frequent storms.

Railways and Shipping Report
I wish to thank my hon. friend from York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) for the following statement which he made in the railways and shipping committee on June 17:
I hare often had to get out at Riviere du Loup in the middle of the night. I have a great deal of sympathy for Mr. Pouliot.
My colleague from Hull (Mr. Fournier) told me that not long ago he visited Riviere du Loup by motor car, and while there he heard a noise on the top of the car. At first he did not know what the trouble was, but eventually learned that the shingles from Riviere du Loup station were dropping on the top of his car.
When the Prime Minister came to Riviere du Loup on July 15, there was a shower, and while standing on the covered platform shaking hands with his friends one of his associates had to hold an umbrella over his head so that he would not be injured by the rain. When His Excellency came to Riviere du Loup, they tried to raise the flag on the station flag-pole, but unfortunately as the pole was broken the flag seemed to be hanging half mast.
Let me now answer some of the objections that have been made by my hon. friend the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion). On March 31, 1931, he said on page 484 of Hansard:
This station was dealt with as were other matters in the constituencies of other hon. members on both sides of the house, as a building program which could not be gone on with , because of the decreased earnings of the Canadian National Railways and because of the large amount of money which this government had to raise for the purposes of the railway.
The same statement was repeated on May 12, 1931. Besides what has been paid for the Montreal terminals in 1930-31, parilament has voted $131,510,400 for capital expenditure of the Canadian National Railways. From September 16 to December 2, 1930, $1,296,483.34 had been approved for new stations by this government. That is 15 times more than $83,271, which was the amount of the lowest tender. The difference between the appropriation and the lowest tender, $6,135, was 94 times or $575,348.34 less than the amount approved by this government for stations not in the Canadian National Railways budget. (Reference No. 314; Hansard, June 25 and June 29).
The second objection of the Minister of Railways was this, at page 1536 of Hansard of May 12, 1931:
My hon. friend seems to have the impression that the station at Riviere du Loup is the only station or the only railway building of any kind which was not built as originally proposed. Such, however, is not the ease.

Of six new stations included in the approved Canadian National Railways 1930-31 budget, it is the only one the construction of which the Department of Railways has refused to sanction, although the same department afterwards approved the construction or completion of five new stations not originally in the approved Canadian National Railways budget. (Reference No. 314, page 4).
The third objection of the Minister of Railways was this. He said, on April 15, 1931, on page 618 of Hansard:
What condition was that cellar in during the five years of the Liberal regime when my hon. friend was sitting behind the cabinet? Why did not my hon. friend have things fixed up during that five years?
In 1925, the first year I was elected, I sent a memorandum to Sir Henry Thornton asking for the building of that station, and I renewed my request every year, but each year Mr Appleton, the general manager at Moncton, replied that the management had to cut expenditures. In 1928 I succeeded in having an amendment made to the law in order to put the old government railways, especially the Intercolonial, under the control of the Board of Railway Commissioners. That is reported in Hansard of April 12, 1928, and of April 23, 1931, at pages 996 and 997. I wish again to thank Hon. Mr. Dunning for the change he made in that respect.
In December, 1928, the Riviere du Loup station was inspected by the provincial board of health, and their report will be found in Hansard of March 31 and of April 15 of this year. The recommendation of the board of health was endorsed in April, 1929, by the chamber of commerce and the city council of Riviere du Loup, as will be found in Hansard of April 15, 1931, at page 614*
On May 1, 1929, Mr. Appleton wrote to the secretary of the chamber of commerce to tell him that it was agreed that the Canadian National Railways would put an item in their budget of 1930 for building a station at Riviere du Loup. In May of 1930 an appropriation of $77,136 was voted in that commotion. That will be found in return 313, and in Hansard of September 19, 1930. Tenders were called for in July, 1930, and I quote from the instructions given in connection with the tendering for the station building at Riviere du Loup, as will be found in reference 425, Hansard, June 22, 1931:
The work covered by this contract shall be commenced immediately the contract is awarded, and all the work shall be fully completed not later than February 28, 1931.

Railways and Shipping Report
On April 23, 1931, I told the Minister of Railways:
If my hon. friend the Minister of Railways were the cleverest lawyer in Canada; if he were as good a lawyer as he is a doctor, I should nevertheless say to him that he has a very bad case.
I was referring to his defence of the decision that had been made.
On April 23 of this year, at page 932 of Hansard, the Minister of Railways said:
So far as I know there is no political patronage in regard to the Canadian National Railways.
I will tell the minister what happened in his absence and in the absence of the Prime Minister. I will give the details of the killing of the proposal to build a station at Riviere du Loup, which is just as interesting as a murder case. At a banquet which took place at Riviere du Loup on December 29, I said:
I am credibly informed that the defeated Tory candidate was in Ottawa on the day when the Department of Railways refused to sanction the construction of the new station at Riviere du Loup. He must have seen the Acting Minister of Railways (Sir George Perley) or communicated directly or indirectly with that department through the Minister of Marine. Either he did not have enough influence to force the minister to reconsider his decision, or he has instigated it. In the first case he is a useless being; in the second case, he is a noxious being.
On January 8, 1931, his companion, Mr. Leo Berube, stated publicly -that I should either prove that statement or retract it. Mr. Berube is a lawyer of note, although he has -been successively defeated in both the counties of Temiscouata and Kamouraska. He took the stand that the Temiscouata Tories were above reproach. I felt sure that I should be allowed at least to see Mr. Dube's correspondence with the Canadian National Railways and the government, and my surprise was indeed great when it was refused me because Mr. Dube was one of those who said that I should either prove or retract my statement. Instead of giving me a chance to get my evidence, he had that correspondence concealed by marking it personal. Is that good sportsmanship?
Now I come to the personal, private and confidential correspondence. On May 7, June 1 and June 16 I was refused the tabling of the correspondence between Mr. Dube and the Canadian National Railways. On June 5 and June 9 the Minister of Railways and the chairman of the railways and shipping committee told me that the answers to my questions would be given in the House of Commons. That will be found in the report of the railways and shipping committee at
pages 5 and 25. On June 10, 1901, at page 2481 of Hansard, the Prime Minister said:
As the matter to which my hon. friend re ferred originated last year, i-t might be considered by the special committee.
The hon. member for Rimouski (Sir Eugene Fiset) replied:
The chairman of the committee has already ruled that as those questions are on the order paper they cannot be discussed in committee.
I observe by reference No. 355 that the Deputy Minister of Railways wrote to the under Secretary of State on June 8, 1901, as follows:
As the correspondence received from Mayor Dube is marked personal it is not brought down.
I personally objected to the non-production of the personal correspondence of that gentleman with the government. Why did he mark personal even letters that had been partly published in the press? In order to learn why, I had to ask numerous questions. With reference to no member of this house, may I be allowed to quote Job, chapter 34, verse 21:
There is no darkness, nor shadow of death, where the workers of iniquity may hide themselves.
The production of that correspondence would have saved lots of time. On August 23 Mr. Dube wrote to Mr. Appleton that the contract should be given to the local contractors, etcetera. That "etcetera" means a lot. There were two tenderers. Dumont & Damours, and Jos. Collin. On March 26 he wires to Mr. Dupre:
Dumont and Damours are Pouliot's strongest followers and friends.
That is in reference number 352. There was only another tender from Riviere du Loup, the tender by Mr. Jos. Collin.
On August 30th he wrote to Mr. Appleton asking for the name of the contractor to get in touch with him.

speechtext: Who is that?

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN THIRD REPORT OF SELECT STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Jos. Collin, a good
Tory from my county. He is advised that the tenders have been sent to Montreal for final decision. Then he is not any more successful in writing to the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion), who had declared in the house it was not in the interest of the country nor of the railway to divulge the amount of each tender, and apparently he has not further satisfied his morbid curiosity. I congratulate the Minister of Railways on his discretion in that respect.
Railways and Shipping Report

On September 4, last year, that gentleman wrote to the Solicitor General:
I will perhaps go to Ottawa during the last week of the special session.
He waited until the Minister of Railways left for Churchill before he came here, for the reason which I have just given.
At what date did Mr. Dube come to Ottawa? According to Hansard of May 28, pages 2040 and 2041.
The Minister of Railways left for Fort Churchill Wednesday, October 1st, returned to Ottawa Saturday, October 11.
In Le Saint Laurent of November 27 the gentleman in question said that while in Ottawa he had had an interview with the Postmaster General, the Minister of Marine and the Minister of Public Works. On the fifteenth of this month the hon. Minister of Marine wrote me as follows-I translate 'his letter for the benefit of the house:
Mr. Dubd reminded me that in effect he had come to Ottawa in the company of Mr. Berube and that these two gentlemen met me, October 6, a Monday, on the train between Montreal and Ottawa. I remember the occasion well.	.	..	,
In our conversation on the tram we discussed general topics. There even may have been mention made of the Riviere du Loup station but not in a way to change what Mr. Dube wrote me on October 2nd. I did not see Mr. Dube and Mr. Berube again-during their stay in Ottawa.
On October 2nd Mr. Dube wrote the Minister of Marine insisting on a new building. He was then favourable to the proposal provided that Mr. Collin was the contractor. The Minister of Marine was at his office in Ottawa on October 6 as will be seen on page 3561 . of Hansard of July 9. Then Messrs. Dube and Berube came with him on the noon train to Ottawa.
What was their purpose in coming here? On August 20 Mr. Dube wrote the Board of Railway Commissioners:
We are very anxious that this station shall be constructed immediately.
The same day he wrote to the Minister of Labour (Senator Robertson):
Authorization shall be given at once to Canadian National Railways to award contract as soon as possible in order that the work should be started without delay.
And naturally he was recommending a local contractor. He sent a copy of that letter to the Prime Minister, the Postmaster General, the Minister of Marine and the Solicitor General. On September 12 he wrote to the Prime Minister:
The contract shall be awarded without delay.
Collin! Collin 1

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN THIRD REPORT OF SELECT STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Who is Mr. Collin?
[Mr. Pouliot.1

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN THIRD REPORT OF SELECT STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Collin is the gentleman who did not get the contract, and because he did not get the contract the station was not built. On October 2nd he wrote to the Minister of Marine:
Nothing shall delay the starting of the work.
On October 4th he wrote to Sir Henry Thornton:
Do all you can to rush that construction.
The travellers suffered a sunstroke on the way to Damascus. Before October 6, everything was going well. On August 9th the Board of Railway Commissioners had issued order No. 45205, reference No. 296, approving plans for the building of the new station. Proposed contracts were forwarded for the consideration of the department after they had been recommended' by the board of directors or by the executive committee of the board of directors. My reference is Hansard of June 22, 1931. What was the resolution? There was a meeting of the executive committee of the Canadian National Railways at Montreal on September 2, 1930. Let me quote:
Submitted to the meeting a memorandum dated August 29 from Mr. Hungerford recommending that a contract be placed with the Stewart Construction Company Limited of Sherbrooke for $83,271-the lowest tenderer-for the construction of station building at Riviere du Loup.
It was unanimously recommended that such a contract be made.
It was declared that the immediate carrying out of the above resolution is required. (Reference No. 449.)
Messrs. Dumont and Damours were not recommended, but an outside firm at Sherbrooke-the same firm that two days later was awarded the contract for the station at Levis. This resolution recommending acceptance was forwarded on September 4th by Mr. Fair-weather to the Department of Railways and Canals.
Speaking at Brandon, Manitoba, in June, 1930, the present Prime Minister is reported in the Winnipeg Evening Tribune of June 23, 1930, as follows:
I want to say that the Conservatives in power will give the Canadian National management a stronger support and a more disinterested support than they have had under the King administration. There will be less log-rolling and interference. The management will be better able to carry out their policies without politicians butting in and trying to stop them.
Everything was O.K. The only thing the travellers had to do was to stay at home to assure the building of a new station at Riviere du Loup, because the plan had been approved by the railway board and the accept-

Railways and Shipping Report
ance of the lowest tender had been recommended by the board of directors; and as the policy of the right hon. Prime Minister was not to interfere with the management of the railway, the station was to be built.
The absent are not always wrong, and I am not putting the blame on the right hon. Prime Minister nor on the Solicitor General because at that time they were at the Imperial conference; the Secretary of State was in Berlin, Germany; the Postmaster General says he has no correspondence in that regard; the Minister of Marine in the letter of July 15 says he did not meet those travellers during their stay in Ottawa; my hon. friend the Minister of Railways was in Churchill. But there was one minister in Ottawa from the province of Quebec-the Acting Prime Minister, who on the 8th of this month said-I am quoting from Hansard, page 3505:
I was not absent from Ottawa a single day during the time the Prime Minister was away from Ottawa last autumn.
Now we come to the second part. While the delegation was in Ottawa on October 6, the matter was before council, although the Minister of Railways was absent from October 1 to 11, as we have seen. In Hansard of May 12, 1931, at page 1538, the Minister of Railways said:
The hon. gentleman has pointed out in this house on a number of occasions that I was up at Fort Churchill when the matter went through council.
In Hansard of June 22, at page 2865, will be found the following:
The matter was still before council when the Minister of Railways and Canals left for Fort Churchill.
According to reference No. 303:
No record can be found of such order in council as referred to by the Minister of Railways and Canals on May 12, 1931, relating to the proposal to build a new station at Riviere du Loup.
On July 16 I put this question on the order
paper:
Was the proposal to build a new railway station at Riviere du Loup put before council?
To which the Prime Minister said:
Mr. Speaker, it has been held that this is an improper question.
Thereupon the Speaker declared the question out of order. The matter was important enough to be submitted to council. Therefore could it be decided otherwise than by order in council? On September 24, Mr. Berube, one of the travellers, wrote to my friend from Dorchester, (Mr. Gagnon):
We must act quickly-II faut faire vite!
On the same day that the travellers arrived in Ottawa the secretary of the Department of Railways and Canals wrote to the Canadian National Railways to the effect that the department had refused to sanction the building of the station. Mr. Pugsley wrote to Mr. Fairweather on October 6:
I am to advise that it has been decided by the department-
I ask hon. members to note those words "by the department."
-not to award a contract for the construction of the proposed new station at Riviere du Loup, but to make repairs, etc.
That is reference No. 295. On October 6 the secretary of the Department of Railways and Canals, "acting upon instructions of the acting deputy minister," notified the Canadian National Railways by letter that the department had refused to sanction the construction of a new station at Riviere du Loup. That is reference No. 315, and Hansard, May 28, 19811. Before leaving for Churchill the Minister of Railways said the matter was still before council and that he did not communicate with anyone during his trip. This will be found at page 3048 of the French Hansard of June 22 and Hansard of May 28, He was accompanied by the deputy minister. It is strange that the acting deputy minister takes, proprio motu, such a step. Is it possible that a matter submitted to council was decided not by council not by the minister in charge, not by the deputy minister, but by the acting deputy minister? On June 22, I asked this question:
Under the authority of what minister, acting minister or person did the Department of Railways and Canals make a decision ....
The minister said he did not think the question was proper, and it was dropped.
What was the meaning of the refusal of October 6? On October 6 the plans had been approved by the Board of Railway Commissioners and the directors of the Canadian National had unanimously recommended the acceptance of the tender, in accordance with Mr. Hungerford's memorandum. On April 23 the minister said "the directors of the railway work in association with the management." Did the management decide to change their views? In reference No. 314 we find the following:
The Riviere du Loup station is the only one that the department refused to sanction the construction of as, it was alleged, there was no necessity for constructing a new station as with proper repairs, additions and improvements the existing accommodation could be made satisfactory.

Railways and Shipping Report
On June 29 I asked if someone had reported after September 4, 1930, that it would be improper to build a new station. The answer was: Reference No. 314 contains no reference to any such report. See Hansard of June 29, page 3134. The first report from the railway is dated December 9, 1930; it is a letter from the assistant chief engineer to Mr. Alastair Fraser as follows:
It is quite correct that the railway called for tenders for a new station at Riviere du Loup, but these were entirely too high and it has therefore been decided to thoroughly renovate the present structure in order to meet the requirements of the travelling public.
It was written two months after the decision was made on October 6. The whole amount of each section of vote No. 323, 1930, totalling $51,600,0000 was not spent until three months later on December 31, 1930 (Reference No. 322); it was not spent on October 6. The assistant chief engineer says the tenders were too high. The lowest tender was nearly $7,000 less than the engineer's estimate, while at Levis a contract was approved having to do with a tender which was more than $6,000 over the engineer's estimate.
At last the cat comes out of the bag. Who made a decision so absurd and so diametrically opposed to the policy preached by the Prime Minister at Brandon? Was it an architect, an engineer or at least a foreman? No, it was the boss, the acting Prime Minister. The following appears at page 3561 of Hansard under date of July 9:
Mr. Pouliot: Who was the minister or the acting minister in charge of the Department of Railways and Canals on October 4, 1930?
Mr. Manion: The acting Prime Minister.
Between October 1 and October 7 there was no aeting_ minister in charge of the Department of Railways, but the acting Prime Minister could act for any minister, at any time, during the absence of the minister, without an order in council being required.
That is in Hansard for June 22, of this year. I asked if the same thing had been done by the same hon. gentleman (Sir George Perley) in other departments, but the question was ruled out of order. I asked how many times the same gentleman had been appointed acting minister, and that question was also ruled out of order.
In Hansard for June 22 I find the following:
Proposed contracts are forwarded for consideration of the department after they have been recommended by the board of directors or by the executive committee of the board of directors.
Tenders were received at Moncton on August 26, and were submitted by the company to the department, the approval of the

department being required because such construction involved a capital expenditure by the Canadian government railways. That is from reference No. 3il7.
Now I should like to discuss the illegality of such unwarranted intrusion by the acting Prime Minister. According to Halsbury, seventh volume, page 46, the Prime Minister acts as the medium of communication between the cabinet and the crown. This means no administrative duties. He is the first amongst equals. In the revised statutes of 1927, chapter 1, section 31 (f) I find the following:
If a power is conferred or a duty imposed on the holder of any office as such, the power may be exereised and the duty shall be performed by the holder for the time being of the office.
Subsection (ll) of the same chapter reads:
Words directing or empowering a minister of the crown to do any act or thing, or otherwise applying to him by his name of office, include a minister acting for, or, if the office is vacant, in the place of such minister, under the authority of an order in council, and also his successors in such office, and his or their lawful deputy.
Chapter 171, section 3, of the revised
statutes of 1027 is as follows:
There shall be a department of the government of Canada which shall be called the Department of Railways and Canals, over which the Minister of Railways and Canals for the time being, appointed by commission under the great seal of Canada, shall preside.
(2) The minister shall have the management and direction of the department, and shall hold office during pleasure.
Section 7 of the same chapter is as follows:
The minister shall have the management, charge and direction of all government railways and canals.
The day after October 6 the acting Prime Minister was appointed by order in council P.C. 2349 as acting Minister of Railways and Canals, and acted as such from October 7 to October 11. Perhaps this was done because the banks refused to finance any corporation which had a contract unless the gentleman who had to approve same was appointed acting minister of that department. In the meantime he submitted to council only one order. On October 8, 1930, P.C. 2370 was passed having to do with orders for additions to the station at Levis. See Hansard, June 1, page 2197. Then, at page 482 of Hansard for March 31, of this year I asked the following question:
Mr. Pouliot: Was he appointed acting Minister of Railways and Canals in order to refuse to sanction the construction work at Riviere du Loup?
Mr. Manion:	Certainly not.

Railways and Shipping Report
This is no joke; if an order in council was necessary for the station at Levis how could the acting Prime Minister decide the case of Riviere du Loup in the absence of the minister, and without consulting him? The acting Prime Minister was not in charge of the department, according to the law of the land. The person who was in charge of the department was the Minister of Railways; he was not in Ottawa but he was in charge of the office, and the action of the acting Prime Minister was an unwarranted intrusion. May I repeat here what I have already said this session, that the right hon. Prime Minister and the Minister of Railways never would have done such a thing or made such a decision, if they had been here at the time.
Let me add that the Prime Minister has only the right of supervision over departments, and I contend that that decision of the acting Prime Minister was illegal and void. The province of Quebec has been kind to my hon. friend (Sir George Perley); he has been elected six times in Argenteuil and I regret that in the sunset of his life he has done such injury to a little town of the province which has done so well for him.
On May 22 the minister of railways said:
I do not intend to be bulldozed by the hon. member.
He forgot that the word "bulldoze", according to Webster, means the intimidation of negro voters in Louisiana. Was there a negro in the wood-pile? No contractor but Collin was to be allowed to build the station. His tender was for $44,864 more than the appropriation, for $38,729 more than the lowest tender and for $31,766 more than the railway estimate. He was "the local contractor" who had been recommended so often by Mr. Dube to the Canadian National and to the government. On October 11, Mr. C. E. Dube sent to the deputy minister of railways a copy of the letter which every contractor tendering on the Riviere du Loup station received. The letter was dated October 7 and was addressed to " Mr. Jos	general contractor, Riviere du
Loup station." The Canadian National were returning his deposit cheque for $2,500 and his employers' liability bond amounting to $10,000. (Reference No. 300). It would be highly interesting to know who were Collin's bondsmen, but at any rate, according to reference No. 466, the bond was returned to Mr. Collin on October 7 last. This person was the highest tenderer, he was guaranteed by bondsmen and Mr. Dube and Mr. Berube argued his case here, but it was impossible
even for the Acting Prime Minister to recommend the acceptance of such an extravagant tender. The conclusion was reached, however, that the station should not be built by anyone else, because the profiteers could not have their chance.
According to reference 314, a decision was arrived at on October 4. I had asked whether on that date any letter, memorandum, note or other document had1 been sent by or had emanated from the member for Argenteuil, in the absence of the Minister of Railways, to the acting deputy minister or to the secretary of the Department of Railways and Canals, with reference to awarding the contract for the construction of the proposed new station at Riviere du Loup. This will be found in Hansard of June 29, 1931, at page 3135. The answer was that there was no such document. On July 8 the right hon. member for Argenteuil said: "I do not keep a diary." On July 13 I inquired whether there had been a sitting of the council on October 4, and the Prime Minister Objected to the question. On July 15 the question was ruled out of order. The 4th was a Saturday and the 6th a Monday, and it is improbable that there was a sitting of council on either of those days. No record can ibe found of such an order in council as referred to by the Minister of Railways in Hansard of May 12, 1931. relating to the proposal to build a new station. (Reference No. 303). There is no written evidence to prove that the decision was made on October 4. Is there not a clerical error in this? It reminds me of the old puzzle: What looks like an egg, is round, like an egg, has a yolk and a shell, and barks? The fellow to whom this puzzle was put replied, of course, "I don't know"; whereupon the answer came, "Why-, it is an egg." The other fellow objected that an egg does not bark and the man who proposed the puzzle explained that that was added to make the puzzle more difficult.
May I say that Mr. Dube and Mr. Berube were still in Ottawa on October 7, when the tenders and deposit cheques were returned. On January 8 Mr. Dube published a letter bearing no date and with the signature of the then Acting Prime Minister, in which it was stated that the writer had not met him for six months. When I asked for the date of the letter the question was ruled out of order. The same ruling was made on July 15, with regard to the request for the production <k the entire correspondence between these two parties.
After the delegation had come here the sum of $475,000 was included in the unemployment scheme for a station at Saint John, New
39y4

Railways and Shipping Report
Brunswick, and the gentleman of whom I spoke said that, as he had not been elected, he had no promise to fulfil, although his correspondence had been referred by the private secretary of the Prime Minister to the Minister of Labour.
There were protests from the chamber of commerce of Riviere du Loup on November 27, as well as from the board of health. These references can be found in Hansard of March 31 and May 22. On March 27, according to a return, reference 4676, which can be found in Hansard of April 15, the railway board reported to the effect that they had rescinded their first order, approving only the plans for repairs. This is the only matter in respect to which I think the Minister of Railways is at fault, for it could not have been decided without his knowledge. I regret this, inasmuch as I do not blame him for some venial sins of inaccuracy. On May 22, at page 1906, the minister said:
If the government requests the Board of Railway Commissioners to give Montreal and other interested districts an opportunity to appear in this matter, the Board of Railway Commissioners would hardly dare take any other course.

When discussing generalities, Mr. Speaker, one seldom comes to a definite conclusion. I have studied a concrete case to learn what had been the relations of the government with the Canadian National Railways in the absence of the Prime Minister and the minister in charge. I regret very much not to have been as pleasant to the acting Prime Minister as was the South American brass band. On May 23, 1931, the correspondent of the Montreal Star wrote:
In tribute to Mr. Pouliot it should be recognized that, while his persistence may not have succeeded in convincing parliament that the Riviere du Loup station is a national issue, it has resulted in directing attention to other important matters to which the discussion has led.

I suggest to the government that they should cover the illegality of the decision of October 6, 1980, by removing the injustice which has been done to a small centre in the province of Quebec. If not, I will come back again session after session, and when I am asked whether I am downhearted, my answer will be, no.

This question of the Riviere du Loup station was brought up in that way before the Minister of Railways left for Churchill. speechtext:
I do not know whether it is possible to get back from Riviere du Loup station to the discussion of the general principles contained in the report which is before us. The hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) gave us the impression that he had made his speech because he wished us to love and not to despise our own railroad. If the hon. member was sincere in that desire it seems to me that he took a very strange way of trying to effect the result. It appears to me that his criticism was most unfair. He took this great public enterprise, the Canadian National Railways, and denounced many of its departments and activities without making any comparison with similar departments and activities of its private competitor. I do not know that any blame can be attached to the Canadian National because it has its own publications. As a matter of fact the Canadian Pacific has its own publications which are very carefully edited and distributed. I do not know that any particular blame can be placed upon, the Canadian National for having its own telegraph system; the private road has its own telegraph system. I do not know that there is anything reprehensible in the Canadian National operating its own radio. As far as the question of hotels is concerned, it may be that it has built too largely and has catered to a certain element in the community more than it should have, but if it has done that it is because of the influence of big business in t'he sphere of private competition. If the hon. member had really intended that we should come to love our own national system he would have offered some constructive criticisms by which we could improve the present method of carrying on the work of the road.
The hon. member criticized the scrutiny made by a committee of this house of the estimates of the Canadian National Railways. It seems to me that the work of this committee is one of the finest pieces of work done
by the house. I was very much interested a few years ago when the government went so far as to set up a committee of this character. It seems to me that we would be well advised to have similar committees discussing the estimates of the other departments. If the estimates of the Canadian National Railways were discussed in the committee of the whole as are the estimates of the other departments, we would be here until next fall. I think it is an excellent idea that hon. members should be given an opportunity to meet the president and higher officials and discuss in detail the expenditures and policies of the company.
We all recognize that public ownership on a scale such as we have in the Canadian National Railways is altogether new in the history of our country. A fair trial should be given to this organization. What does the hon. member for Stanstead propose as an alternative to existing arrangements? Would he bring back the old patronage system which existed in the days of the Intercolonial railway? I do not think any hon. member would seriously consider that that is the best way to conduct our business. Does the hon. member mean that we should turn over our own road to a private corporation? If he does, why does not he come out and say so instead of trying to persuade this house that he is trying to get us to love our own road? If I have any criticism to make of the Canadian National road and its management, it is that we copy too closely the methods in vogue in private corporations. It is well known that we took over private companies which had become bankrupt. If we had built from the ground up things might have been different, but we all know that it was to save what was left from private enterprise in which there had been multiplications of all sorts that the Canadian National was organized, and gradually developed into the present system.
The hon. member for Stanstead states that those charged with the management of the road know nothing about railroads, they would not know a hay rake from a handcar. That may be a catchy phrase which may be picked up by the press but-

The hon. member pointed out a fact which I think is evident to everyone, that there is not sufficient business to maintain the road up to its present standard. That is equally true in the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway, but it was not pointed out that in either case the charges must be borne by the people of this country. The idea is so often expressed that it is only in the case of the Canadian National that the taxpayer has to pay when, as a matter of fact, it is equally
(Mr. Woodsworth.]
true of the Canadian Pacific. That railway managed to store away large reserves, some of them hidden, and now in a time of crisis they bring forth those reserves in order to continue partly to pay their regular dividends. That may be legitimate business, but none the less those dividends are being taken out of the pockets of the people who use the railroad. It is a charge on the industry of this country. It is all very well to say that the railroads should pay their way, but they have never done so. If the Canadian Pacific had been left to finance and push through its road, I do not suppose it ever would have been pushed through to completion. We know that enormous grants in land and money were made to the Canadian Pacific, and we know that at that time there was a Pacific scandal comparable to the Beauharnois scandal of the present day. After reading the report and hearing something of the discussion, it seems to me that one of our chief difficulties lies in this, that because of the competition of the government road with the private road a great many expenditures have been forced upon the public road. Then, again, there is another reason for this large expenditure. I think that to too large an extent the public-owned road has been copying the practices that are prevalent among private corporations. I note that among the recommendations of the committee there is one that, where possible, we should reduce the expenditure on operation and maintenance. We will all agree with that, stated in such general terms, but I hope the committee did not have in mind a reduction in wages; that is the wrong end at which to begin. All our economists to-day are telling us that one of the difficulties in our modern economic structure is that we have given too little in the way of wages and services, and allowed too much in the form of capital expenditure.

I know there was

It has reduced wages to a very small extent, and it has not cut off its employees to nearly like the same extent as the privately owned road. On the part of some that policy has been the ground of criticism against the Canadian National Railway.
In reviewing this report may I urge then that while in a general way we ought to try

to reduce expenditures, we ought not to permit a reduction of wages. The chairman of the committee has referred to the special section dealing with salaries. Perhaps I might be permitted to read that:
In view of the decreased revenues of the company, and the economies being made in other branches of the service, your committee are of opinion that the executive committee of the board of directors should immediately consider the whole question of salaries, allowances, disbursements, pensions and retirement provisions for executive officers and officials of the company receiving salaries of $5,000 and over, in order that every reasonable and proper economy should be effected.
