I was mentioning
just now what I thought was one omission. There are two clauses to which I should like to call attention, if only to underline them. Some of us from the west, and I should like to speak for some of the members from the west as the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) has spoken for some of the people in Ontario, feel very strongly on this matter of public ownership. Some of us do feel that there has been some slackness in the expenditures of the Canadian National. Some of us feel that there have been expenditures which were not justified, although in faimes3 it may be said that comparatively only a short time ago we were passing through almost boom times when no expenditure was considered too great. There were these large expenditures on hotels, and so forth, which in my judgment were quite unjustified, and which catered to one particular section of the community rather than to the masses of the people. There are two brief sections in the report which I have marked. One reads:
Your committee while of opinion that many of the salaries are much too generous, and in some instances excessive, accede to the expressed wish of the president that the list be not published for the reasons given by him.
If I understand it aright, the reason for not publishing the list is the reason usually advanced by private companies, that it is a matter of private business and ought not to be given out to the general public. Now, as most hon. members know, I am decidedly in favour of publicity in such matters; I do not think that publicity is dangerous. I can quite well see, however, the difficulties in this particular matter because we are dealing only with our own road. It might very well be that with no basis for comparison the mere publication of certain figures might be mis-

understood or misinterpreted. I can understand the viewpoint which was held by a considerable number of members in committee. I cannot however see why the time should not come when the higher salaries in the Canadian Pacific Railway ought not to be published just as much as those in the Canadian National Railway. After all when a road receives so much from the public as does the Canadian Pacific Railway, when it can go to the railway board and ask that freight rates be maintained in order that it may keep up its dividends, I say that the details of the business of the road should no longer be private. There is no good reason why the larger salaries on the Canadian Pacific Railway should not be published side by side with those of the Canadian National Railways.
Then there is the further sentence:
Your committee strongly condemn the practice which has grown up under which the Canadian National Railways are chargeable with large amounts for payment of the social entertainment and other activities of officials on other than official business.
Again let me say that in that regard I should like to endorse the findings of the committee. It seems to me that the practice described in the sentence I have just read is most reprehensible. We are all aware that practices of that sort are commonly indulged in by other great corporations, and the excuse is often made that under our present competitive system unless our road did that sort of thing it might lose business. I do not know if that argument is sound but I do know it is often advanced as one reason why our road in competition with others should resort to such practices. Be that as it may, since the road is government owned, surely scrutiny cannot be too careful or detailed.
I should like to express my hearty concurrence in the recommendations by the committee. My hope is that we may lop off those things which are inimical to the best interests of the road. If housecleaning has to be done, we will have to do that housecleaning, but we must not endanger the general principle underlying the great public utilities of which we are justly proud.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN THIRD REPORT OF SELECT STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The observations of the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett), to which the house listened this afternoon, reflect only his own personal views. It is the privilege, I take it, of any hon. member when the report of a committee is presented to make such observations as he may desire to make concerning any particular public matter.

Railways and Shipping Report
In conformity with that practice the hon member for Stanstead has expressed hig opinions. They were stated in terms which represented his own views, and his own views only so far as this government is concerned, with respect to the matters about which he spoke.
I do not purpose to discuss the report or to say more than this, that since I have had the responsibilities of office no matter has given me more concern or pressed more heavily upon me than has the railway situation in Canada. I do think, as I have so frequently said, that it is time hon. members studied the situation in all its ramifications; for we are a people only 10,000,000 in number with railway facilities far beyond our requirements. We have an enterprise owned by the people of Canada who acquired if under circumstances to which I shall not refer this afternoon. In competition with a privately owned road they have endeavoured to maintain that railway system. They have placed money into its operation with great freedom and willingness; they have backed it with a courage and determination which I think at least has satisfied those who had to administer the railroad that nothing any government has done in this country has stood in the way of every reasonable effort being made to advance the fortunes of the railroad When the opportunity comes to discuss the affairs of the railway company I am sorry to find that there is a group which thinks that any criticism constitutes adverse criticism of the ownership of the road. That has not been so. Surely, however, for the same reasons that hon. members criticize expenditures by departments and estimates submitted by ministers, in the very nature of things there should be free criticism with respect to every matter connected with the administration of our own property. If the hon. member for Stanstead expressed his personal views I can only say that he has not expressed the views of the government or those I hold personally. For instance, the board of directors may be all that he says they are. For my part I think they are a reasonable crosssection of the Dominion of Canada, and that in every reasonable way, taking them man for man, they represent the whole of Canada. They are men from every walk of life, men experienced in corporate management, professional men or farmers. If one were to take the trouble to analyze their records he would find that those directors represent in a general way the people of Canada.
Traffic conditions are bad-very bad. Those conditions however are not confined to
our own road but exist as well in respect to other roads. It is unfortunate that the mere discussion of a situation should resolve itself into recriminations between individuals. I think the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) was correct when he said that the report of the committee represents a compromise of conflicting opinions. The fact that it was unanimous was to me a matter of great personal gratification, because I had followed the proceedings of the committeo only in a casual way, and when I saw that a unanimous opinion had been arrived at 1. thought the members of the committee were to be congratulated, and the country was to be congratulated upon the fact that it was possible for the committee to arrive at a unanimous opinion. In fact what has been said to-day has only strengthened my personal views.
I think if the house will take the trouble to analyze what has been done since the present government came into office and the effort it has made to maintain the integrity of the property consistently with the obligations which in the end must be borne by the Canadian people, hon. members will be satisfied that no step has been taken other than for the purpose of advancing its well being and proper management. It does not follow, however, that in so doing, hon. members will agree wrholly with everything that has been done; for certainly there are many hon. members who will join in the criticisms urged in the report with respect to those three steamships on the Pacific coast. The answer is, however, that this parliament agreed to their operation. It is much to be regretted that we have those three vessels losing such tremendous sums of money and serving no useful purpose. My only difficulty has been to understand how it was possible that they should have been constructed. They are there, however, and we have to deal with the situation as it exists.
I fancy the hon. member for North Waterloo realizes that criticism of that nature is sound and constructive. At the same time there is some force in what was said by the hon. member for Stanstead, that it is pathetic to think we must always be too late. All the thinking in the world will not unscramble that situation. It is there, and our business is to try to meet it. I put it to the members of this house fairly that it is rather an intolerable burden, isn't it, when in addition to trying to provide for the financial situation of the country you have to carry a load with respect to the railways, and find yourself saddled from month to month and from day

Railways and Shipping Report
to day with enormous deficits with respect to the operation of something which a committee of the house think never should have had being? That is a reflection upon all of us, upon this parliament and every hon. member who was in it when the arrangements were made, and upon every government which has had to do with it. There is no doubt that thoughtful people are beginning to realize that fact and to ask questions about it. I realize that in the very nature of things you must expect mistakes to be made; 86,000,000 or $7,000,000 is a big mistake and it takes a lot of money, it takes an enormous amount of traffic to pay the interest on it. When you realize that the boats are not earning their operating costs, not enough to pay for the fuel, the oil, the wages of the crew and the upkeep, it becomes a serious matter. If criticism of that kind is made in a committee of this house-as it was-and that committee arrives at a unanimous opinion -as it did-I think the committee is to be commended for the action it has taken.
I did not intend to make such a lengthy statement because I am not going to discuss the merits or the demerits of the many matters referred to this afternoon. It suffices for my purposes that a committee of this house, representing all parties, having considered thoughtfully and carefully-in so far as it is possible in a limited time thoughtfully and carefully to consider an undertaking of such magnitude with activities which extend not only throughout every province but also into several of the states of the American union- having so considered these matters, have arrived at a report which is unanimous, and I hope it will be unanimously adopted by the house. For no change in policy can ever take place in respect to this publicly owned property unless the people of Canada, speaking through this parliament, so determine, and there has been no evidence of that so far as I have seen.
But I should like to remind those who, like the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Woodsworth), talk strongly about a certain policy with respect to the ownership of property, that they must never forget that the true test which in the end will determine the success or failure of the venture is the efficiency and effectiveness of the management; and unless we can get the same efficiency and effectiveness in the management of our own property that private enterprises command in theirs, we cannot succeed. The hon. member for North Waterloo put that very fairly the other day, it struck me. I think that is true. We must get it in our minds that the stake we are playing for is 
really the success or failure of the great undertaking upon which the Canadian people embarked some years ago, and which succeeding governments have been endeavouring to maintain in a successful manner. If there are differences of viewpoint by successive administrations, I am sure the common sense of the Canadian people will realize that it is not because one party is viewing the undertaking from one angle and another from another; but that the method of approach as to efficiency and economy on the one hand differs from the method of approach as to efficiency and economy on the other hand. That this house must exercise increasing control with respect to expenditures is only axiomatic when you come to contemplate what vast sums are involved, and how they concern every taxpayer in this Dominion. The success of the whole venture rests upon the efficiency of its management; and the efficiency of its management is reflected by the attitude of this parliament, whose members represent the shareholders; for it is an unfortunate fact-I directed the attention of this house to it many years ago-that the only place where the shareholders of this great enterprise can make themselves vocal is in this chamber. That is, we, two hundred and forty-five members, are the shareholders' spokesmen, their proxies and representatives, at the only form of annual meeting that counts so far as this enterprise is concerned. If, seized of that sense of responsibility, we approach the matter from that angle, I think we shall appreciate that the committee did attempt to reconcile divers opinions and opposing views with the purpose of arriving at constructive suggestions and recommendations, and then present a unanimous report. In that sense I think it is an achievement of which the committee can well be proud, and I commend the report to the consideration of every member. But I would not deny to any member on this side or the other the right to express any opinion he feels, 'but I should like it clearly understood that in so doing he represents his own opinion and not the opinion of myself or of any member of this administration.

speechtext:
I thank my
hon. friend. I have but a few remarks to make. The Prime Minister has referred to the anxiety he has experienced since coming into office with respect to this great railway problem. I am sure he could not feel that his anxiety on that score was any greater than was my own at the time, nearly ten years ago, when the Liberal administration assumed office and was confronted with the railway problem that existed at that time. There were then three different railroads or systems, each of which was in considerable difficulties, but all of which have since been combined into the one great Canadian National Railway system. We found that the Grand Trunk Railway system, because of its being in a state of bankruptcy, had been taken over as a government railway by the preceding administration. It was under its old management and control. We found the Canadian Northern Railway, then a part of the government railway system, also under separate management. We found the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, also a part of the government railway system, in the hands of a receiver. The task which confronted the then administration was to bring those three systems-including the old Intercolonial- into one great national system, to find a president who would be a competent executive, and to arrange for a board of directors.
The problem, in a word, was a choice between a monopoly on the one hand or government ownership competing with private ownership on the other. That was the alternative which had to be faced at the outset-whether we should seek to bring about a combination of all the railways in Canada in one great monopoly, and whether that monopoly should be privately owned or government owned. To the government of the day it seemed that the wisest course was to avoid monopoly and to have competition between the privately owned company and the publicly owned company; we believed that as a matter of fact competition would be good for both, that government ownership would have its best trial were it placed in a position of competition with an efficiently run, privately owned system, and that a privately owned system such as the Canadian Pacific Railway would find itself also aided through the force of competition with an efficiently run government owned system.
The decision being to establish of the three * railway systems first mentioned a government owned railway system, the next problem to be considered was whether that system should be run by the government under political influence or control, or whether it should as
far as possible be removed from such influence and control. The decision reached was to remove the system from government control just as far as was consistent with the circumstances mentioned by my right hon. friend, namely that the people of the country themselves were the shareholders of the system. In establishing the government owned system the object of the government was to give government ownership a fair trial. That was the way in which the policy of the government of the day was presented to the country, and we felt that it would not have a fair trial if there were government interference in the management of the road.
Once it had made up its mind as to the policy to be pursued, the government sought to secure as president and executive head of the new system the best executive that it might be possible to find. It took some little time to discover a competent executive head, but I venture to say that the people of Canada to-day will agree that, having searched a great part of the world as we did, had we searched the world over we could not have found anyone who, in the period of years which has since elapsed, would have given more satisfaction than Sir Henry Thornton has given in the management of the affairs of the road. With Sir Henry Thornton we associated a board of directors, and in order that the system might be free from government control the president and board of directors were given to understand that it was their business to run the Canadian National Railways just as Mr. Beatty and his directors ran the Canadian Pacific Railway. That was the ground on which the position was accepted by Sir Henry and it was the declared policy of the government, the purpose being, as I have said, to give government ownership the fairest trial possible, altogether free from political interference.
Now may I say that it was not without some misgivings that the government entrusted to any group the complete management and control of this great system, misgivings as to the expenditures which might be made, and as to the improvements, extensions and the like which might be requested. There was the further difficulty with respect to any program of railway construction and the like, that not only did the board have to determine its own policy but the administration of the day had to be relied upon to get that policy through this parliament. On more than one occasion, as hon. gentlemen will remember, the board did submit to parliament a plan which they believed to be necessary and which they thought would be most

Railways and Shipping Report
effective. There was for instance the branch line program, which we succeeded in passing through this house but which was defeated in another house. Thereby the railway was prevented from carrying out, at the time thought most desirable, some of the improvements and extensions which the management believed would have advanced the System.
The point I wish to make at the moment is that the government gave to the president and board of directors a free hand; we sought to keep them free from any attempt at political control, and I have yet to hear mention of any influence the government of the day sought to bring to bear upon Sir Henry Thornton and his board of directors other than that of restriction with respect to some of the expenditures they wished to make. It may be, as my right hon. friend has said, that some expenditures have been indulged in that could have been prevented. Some things may have gone a little further than might have been the case if this house had been controlling affairs. No matter who might have been in control there would have been room for criticism. The main point is that the railways have had a chance under government ownership, free from political control, and now we have before us an object lesson as to the possibilities of government ownership on a large scale, as contrasted with the possibilities of private ownership.
May I say that with the greater part of what my right hon. friend has said this afternoon in relation to the report now before the house I am in entire agreement. Personally I am pleased that the committee have found it possible to make a unanimous report; personally I do not regret any criticism which they may have made of what seemed to them extravagance, or of what they have felt to be necessary in the way of cutting down certain expenditures. I know that personally so far as the merchant marine was concerned, I often felt it was very questionable whether those ships should be continued in service year after year at a loss. But it was pointed out to the administration that the Canadian Pacific Railway had vessels afloat which connected its land transportation system with other countries by water routes, and that for the Canadian National Railways to be denied a similar right would be to restrict and handicap that line to the benefit of its great competitor. Arguments of the kind prevailed. If the committee have come to
(Mr. Mackenzie King.]
the conclusion, after the experiment has been tried and it has been made apparent that in these particulars the cost is too great, that it will be the part of wisdom to discontinue these services, personally I am inclined to feel that they have given the matter very careful and full consideration, and that their report in that regard should be adopted. As the Prime Minister has said, the committee have gone into the matter in a more detailed manner than is possible in this house at this time. Studying the report as I have, in the light of such knowledge as I have gained in watching the developments of the last ten years, I am inclined to feel that the note of caution which the committee have sounded to the Canadian National Railways, in the matter of limiting its outlays, is very wise. In saying this, I should also say that had there been any attempt on the part of the administration of that day to interfere with the views of the president, and board of directors as to what was most in the interests of the road, the criticism at the time, or today would not have been directed against the Canadian National Railways, but would have been levelled very directly at the late government for having interfered with a government owned system.

speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, July 17, the debate on the motion of Mr. Lawson for the consideration of Bill No. 118, to incorporate Service Loan and Finance Corporation.

subtopic: SERVICE LOAN AND FINANCE CORPORATION
speechtext: There seem to have been more misstatements with respect to this bill than there have been with regard to any other bill that has been before this house since I have been here.

subtopic: SERVICE LOAN AND FINANCE CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, is the hon.
member closing the debate?

subtopic: SERVICE LOAN AND FINANCE CORPORATION
speechtext: I take it he is. If any other hon. members wish to speak they should do so now.

subtopic: SERVICE LOAN AND FINANCE CORPORATION
speechtext:
I am very sorry that the hon. member for West York (Mr. Lawson) had not the opportunity of explaining this bill, which I think needs a good deal of explaining. Possibly after he had explained the bill I might have changed my opinion with respect to the way I would vote on it should the question come up for a vote to-day. An hon. member, in expressing his opinion on this bill which is now before the house, spoke to me privately of the odious odour cast off by a vicious rodent which he thought was hidden somewhere among its objectionable sections. I asked him what he thought of the principle of the bill and his answer was, " Principle? There is no principle in this bill; but I smell a rat and I think it should be destroyed."
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not know what rats smell like, nor should I care to smell one even if I did suddenly discover its presence in this bill. So far as I am concerned, rats, A1 Capone and exorbitant money lenders all smell alike. There is, however, one service which the rat could perform by virtue of its presence in this bill: it could chew the bill up holus bolus, preamble, principle, sections and all, and then make a hasty retreat from this house down Parliament hill, ending its own hideous life as well as the life of the bill at the bottom of the Ottawa river. I think that by this time I have made myself quite plain where I stand on the bill.
Now I have said that I am not aware of the presence of any rat, nor have my nostrils communicated to my mind any inkling of the nature of the beast. But I do see in my mind's eye drops of blood trickling from a
pound of flesh held aloft in the hands of those people who would profit by this bill should hon. members present to-day allow it to pass this house. I do not smell a rat, but I do see clots of blood and pieces of flesh smeared and dangling everywhere, the nauseous odour of which even now emanates so strongly from the bill that has been sponsored by the hon. member for West York.
The bill, on the face of it, looks innocent enough; but it is said' that the devil is not so bad to look upon if he has a definite place to go and is dressed up in his holiday clothes. The sponsor of this bill would have us believe that the trouble with those who oppose it is that they do not understand it. That is exactly what the woman said when she could not get along with her supposedly worse half -"my husband does not understand me." The hon. member for West York would also have us believe that the bill calls for a paltry seven per cent. That looks lean enough at first sight, but there is more than seven per cent in the bill. To tell the truth, I do not like the bill's hungry look. It looks too ominous to me. It is not so much what this bill says as what it leaves unsaid. The bill does not say, for instance, that a possible seventeen per cent might be charged, but we have the word of the superintendent of insurance as to that potentiality.
May I for a moment digress to ask who the sponsor of the bill may be. I am informed that he is one of nature's noblemen from West York. Look at his kind and genial face, the intelligent features, the broad and noble brow, the light and graceful figure. Can it be that the hon. member who sits over yonder, who has been destined to sit with the mighty, would lend the powers of his intellect to a scrap of paper that is not worth his fettle and that has neither truth nor poetry m it? Is it possible, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for West York does not realize the real import of the bill?
I am still very sorry that the hon. member had no opportunity to give us any further explanation that he might have with respect to the sections of this bill. It is therefore with reluctance in my mind and with alacrity in my heart that I am forced to admit that another promising young member of this house has gone astray. If the hon. member for West York has not yet seen the error of his ways, I would beseech him to repent before it is too late; and if he has any tears to shed I hope he prepares to shed them now. For what the hon. member for West York is doing by sponsoring this bill is virtually putting himself in the place of the rest of

Loan and Finance Corporation
the would-ibe Shyloeks behind it who are seeking to obtain the sanction and authority of law, and who, having obtained it must now needs whet their knives to cut the forfeiture from the inevitable bankrupts that would be Tendered thereby.
I invite hon. members again to turn their gaze to yonder end of the chamber, in the direction of yonder sponsor of the bill, and try to conjure in their minds a picture of said member whetting his knife on the sole of his shoe and testing its sharpness with one of his long scraggly hairs. Like myself I think you -would find it very hard to visualize the dapper young man from West York in any other shape or form than can be seen right now with the naked eye. However, wittingly or unwittingly his support of this bill clothes him with a character which he does not and should not possess. This bill is like the Irishman, it does not know when it is licked. It has been beaten to death and thrown out of the select standing committee on banking and commerce and now it is sneaking back into this chamber virtually asking hon. members to subject it to another annihilation. I wonder whether this bill has as many lives as a cat? If I knew that it had more I would be constrained to speak a little bit longer than I originally intended. It has been killed already but thanks to the serum injected into it by its sponsor, it has come back to life again. It is like the bad penny, always turning up.
It is like the notorious gentleman across the line, A1 Capone, full of scars and other bad features, seeking the protection of law in order to carry on his nefarious work. A1 Capone got rid of his enemies by mowing them down with machine guns. By means of powder, lead and gim, Capone rid himself of One-Eyed Ike, the killer, Snaky Joe the blackmailer and Bugs Moran the would-be bootlegger king. If I have not named the gentlemen correctly I hope some hon. member will put me right because I am not an authority on these matters. However, suffice it to say, that they were done away with because they stood in the way of Capone's ascension to power as chief cook and bottle *washer in his own neck of the woods. Likewise Bill No. 118 does not intend to tolerate any rivals because in paragraph (b) of subsection 1 of section 5 we read the following:
The company may throughout Canada-[DOT]
(b) notwithstanding anything contained in the Interest Act, or in the Money Lenders Act, or in paragraph (c) of section sixty-three of the Loan Companies Act-
(i)	lend money secured by assignment of choses-in-action. chattel mortgages or such other

evidence of indebtedness as the company may require, and may charge interest thereon at the rate of not more than seven per centum per annum, and may on all loans deduct the interest in advance and provide for repayments in weekly, monthly or other uniform repayments: Provided that the borrower shall have the right to repay the loan at any time before the due date, and, on such repayment being made, to receive a refund of such portion of the interest paid in advance as has not been earned, except a sum equal to the interest for three months,
(ii) charge, in addition to interest as aforesaid, for all expenses which have been necessarily and in good faith incurred by the company in making or renewing a loan authorized by the next preceding subparagraph (i), including all expenses for inquiry and investigation into the character and circumstances of the borrower, his endorsers, co-makers or sureties, for taxes, correspondence and professional advice, and for all necessary documents and papers, two per centum upon the principal sum loaned,
This bill would first get rid of its enemies. Enemy No. 1 is the Interest Act; enemy No.
2	is the Money Lenders Act, and enemy No.
3	is the Loan Companies Act. In justice to this bill it must be said that it does not murder these acts, it merely ignores them contemptuously. A1 Capone puts his enemies on the spot and then snuffs them out forever more; this bill just takes them off the spot and renders them impotent. It adds insult to injury by saying to the aforementioned acts: You're only a trio of palookas, deadbeats and has-beens who do not mean a thing in my life. To all this the hon. member for West York chants "Amen." After taking it3 enemies, as it were, for a ride, the bill then goes on to state how it is going to hold up the public. It starts out innocently enough with the statement that all that will be asked is a measly seven per cent, but as we go on we see the said sum swelling up like the pumped fiat tire of a tourist's bus. This bill has contracted another old Capone custom, that of collecting toll. It has contracted the disease of the gimmes; it has "gimme this," "gimme that" and "gimme the other thing."

speechtext: I rise to a point of order. I submit that the hon. member has no right to compare legislation sponsored by another hon. member to the methods used by A1 Capone.

subtopic: SERVICE LOAN AND FINANCE CORPORATION
speechtext: The house has no information as to what A1 Capone is.

subtopic: SERVICE LOAN AND FINANCE CORPORATION
speechtext:
I am merely trying to convey to the house the nefarious character of the legislation we are asked to pass. The veason I have compared it to A1 Capone is

Loan and Finance Corporation
because he is the best parallel of which I know. I have just as little use for A1 Capone as has the hon. gentleman who just interrupted me. 1 have said that this bill has contracted the disease of the gimmes. In other words it would do exactly what A! Capone is doing in Chicago. The charges permitted by this bill seem to be unlimited. I might point out that the company behind this bill is operating already under a provincial charter but it wants to extend its tentacles to the rest of Canada. That is just another old Capone custom; he, not being satisfied with his native haunts of Cicero, must extend his operations to the other wards of Chicago. The seven per cent mentioned in this bill is too much like the old ditty of the spider and the fly to be genuine. The company, being the spider, virtually says to the people, who are flies, what is exemplified by the following verse:
Will you walk into my parlour Said the spider to the fly,
'Tis the prettiest little parlour That ever you did spy.
My advice to the people of Canada and to hon. members of this house is:
But if the fly is wise He never would go in;
He would know very well There was nothing there for him.
That just about expresses my opinion with respect to the bill that is now before the house. Another hon. member on Friday last said that this company would lend only to endorsers and that the main security on which it would lend money was simply that of two co-signers. But how about section 5 of the bill which reads:
The company may throughout Canada:-
(a) buy, sell, deal in and lend money on the security of conditional sales agreements, lien notes, hire purchase agreements, chattel mortgages, trade paper, bills of lading, warehouse receipts, bills of exchange and choses-in-action; and may receive and accept from the makers, vendors or transferors thereof guarantees or other security for the performance and payment thereof and may enforce such guarantees and realize on such security;
Does that section which I have just read justify the supposed innocence which the hon. member for West York, the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Willis), and some other hon. members who spoke on Friday night would attribute to this bill? Not if the inevitable word means anything.
This bill has already been killed in the banking and commerce committee. It now comes stalking back into this chamber like a ghost to haunt hon. members and to call forth nightmares in what otherwise would have been their more or less peaceful sleep.
I repeat, I do not like this bill's lean and hungry look. I like neither its principle nor its provisions. Furthermore, I do not think this is an opportune time to pass a bill of this kind. When the majority of the people of Canada are clamouring for cheaper credit, for the nationalization of our banks, for an equalization of agriculture with other industries, for the suspension of the redemption of Dominion notes in gold, for the depreciation of our currency, and consequently for increased purchasing power, it seems to me that it is the height of audacity to ask parliament at this time to pass legislation the only result of which can be to fatten the pocketbooks of a small group of shareholders at the expense of a duped and unsuspecting public. It is said that these three acts, the Interest Act, the Moneylenders Act, and the Loan Companies Act, are somewhat in the nature of a financial bible. We will call the Interest Act the Bible, the Money Lenders Act the Koran, and the Loan Companies Act the Talmud. Surely nobody but the devil would like to get rid of three such books as those, and I think it is very devilish for this act to try to get rid of such noble acts as we have passed in parliament in times gone by. At a time like this, the house should not countenance a bill of this nature. It is not so long ago that one of the ablest men in the House of Commons, a very brilliant minister on the other side of the house, had a great deal to say about credit. I quoted from a report in one of the newspapers:
In the meantime Hon. Robert Weir, federal minister of agriculture, has been engaging with the banks in a debate over credits to farmers who have still substantial equities in their farms, own stock and implements and buildings, but who have because of low prices run out of ready cash for winter supplies and spring operations. The strength of Mr. Weir's position is that he was recently out west and while there was given authenticated cases of refusal by banks to loan money even where the security was of a high type.
The banks have answered him by challenging him to produce the evidence of what he alleged, but that does not embarrass Mr. Weir, because he has the goods in his office here.
I wish he would show the goods to the hon. member for West York:
He is taking his time in answering the banks because he has been invited to speak in Montreal to the Canadian Club next Monday on the western situation, and to the business men of that city he will quote verse and chapter to prove his assertions.
I hope he will quote verse and chapter also to the hon. member for West York:
Mr. Weir's object is not that of developing sectional feeling or of castigating the banks, but of taking away a weapon which he feels may otherwise become a powerful one in the

Loan and Finance Corporation
hands of professional western agitators, w'ho are making hay while the sun of prosperity is in temporary eclipse. The federal minister is determined to see that the western farmer who is reasonably entitled to help gets it, and has warned that if tile banks will not provide such assistance, someone else will.
Does that, jibe with what the hon. member for West York would have us believe to-day in respect of the bill now under consideration? I do not think it does. I think that he could take a good lead from one of the most billiant ministers on the other side of the house.
I wish to quote from another newspaper about what happened to a fanner out west, because I think it is relevant to the question under consideration, and I wonder how this bill would help a farmer such as the one I am going to read about. I believe that hon. members are already acquainted with this story, but it is so powerful in its influence upon the argument I am advancing that I cannot refrain from quoting it again:
The story concerns a farmer in the Vegre-ville district of northern Alberta, who was required to make immediate delivery of certain grain which had been assigned to the bank as security for a past-due note. Obedient to the banker's instructions, the farmer forthwith hauled the first load to the elevator, but it was pronounced of low grade and rejected on account of its moisture condition.
The farmer was in a quandary both as to what he should do about his rejected grain and his past-due note, when suddenly an inspiration struck him. He had assigned the grain to the bank. The bank had demanded settlement of his note and, since the elevator had refused to accept the grain for storage, the logioal thing to do was to deliver it to Hie bank.
Accordingly he drove over to the bank, backed up to the rear door, and before police arrived he had succeeded in shovelling the bulk of the grain in on the bank floor. He still has the past-due note and is $25 poorer, this being tile penalty exacted for illegal tender.
There is a sequel, however, even to this. Having reloaded the grain, Mr. Farmer was still at a loss as to how he should dispose of it. This problem he solved by dumping it by the roadside as he proceeded back to his farm. Thus the episode would have closed, but for the fact that a neighbour's horse spied the wheat, ate it. swelled up and died. Now the liero of the story faces a suit for damages.
I wonder to what extent a farmer in that situation would be benefited by the bill now before us? It is hard enough to-day for any farmer in the west, to get a loan from a mortgage company or bank, let alone a company like this which is going to charge, not 7, but 17 per cent, according to the evidence of the superintendent of insurance before the banking and commerce committee. I think hon. members would like also to know the view of the farmers with respect to the matter

of credit. Let me read from a resolution passed in the city of Calgary on July 23, 1931:
That we as delegates assembled recognizing the inadequacy of the existent credit system in meeting present economic stringency and believing that adequate distribution of credit is absolutely essential to the carrying on of the agricultural industry recommends:
(1)	That this organization continue to advocate at all times the complete nationalization of our credit system.
(2)	That as an immediate measure the federal government take steps to organize a federal reserve bank of issue and discount which bank shall be entirely under government control and shall provide credit at a reasonable rate of interest for all necessary productive and commercial enterprises.
We are convinced that the above proposal is imperative in order to get away from the present intolerable position in which the credit requirements of the public in general are sacrificed to the professed necessity of the charter banks to protect to the utmost their savings deposits.
(3)	We specifically recommend that the directors of the wheat pool should thoroughly canvass the possibility of their financing the marketing of their grain through utilization and extension of our present finance act.
A further resolution was passed relevant to the matter of interest:
Interest: In view of the present prices of farm products this convention recognizes that the accumulation of interest at the rates charged by many credit organizations constitute an intolerable burden and will greatly delay the return of agriculture to normal conditions and urges
(1)	That the federal government by appropriate legislation definitely fix a maximum legal rate of interest which may be collected in any proceedings with adequate penalties for non-compliance.
(2)	That as soon after this convention as possible the executive confer with the various organizations of creditor interests with a view to effecting voluntary reductions or remission of interest rates on overdue accounts.
(3)	That in the event of the failure of these negotiations the government concerned be urged to pass such measures as may be necessary to meet this situation by way of compulsory adjustment.
(4)	That this convention protest against the prevailing practice of the charter bank charging higher rate of interest for doing business in western Canada than in eastern Canada, and that every effort be taken by the organization both by conference with the banks and by recommendations to the government to remove this inequality.
Notwithstanding this resolution, if the bill now before us were allowed to pass the company would be in a position to extend its tentacles out of the poorer sections of Alberta.

Mr. Speaker, in spite of the fact that apparently the hon. member for Yegreville (Mr. Luchko-vich) intended to compliment me upon my intellectual powers I regret that I am not sufficiently nimble witted to follow through the maze of his mixed metaphors the ideas which in the main he was endeavouring to express in connection with the bill.
I shall not ask the house to consider the bill either from the standpoint of my intellect or my personal appearance but rather on the merits of the bill itself. I had endeavoured to avoid taking up the time of the house in a discussion of the bill by moving that it be recommitted to the select standing committee on banking and commerce where I think its provisions might have been more properly and readily discussed than in the house. But as my hon. friends either by the use of vituperous language or strong statements and allegations have seen fit to cause a discussion in the house on the bill I crave the indulgence of hon. members for a few moments in order that I may lay before them what I conceive to be the intention and purposes of the proposed legislation.
In so doing may I at the outset ask hon. members to bear in mind that the bill now before them is in terms almost identical with those of two or three bills of incorporation which were previously passed by this parliament. In one case legislation was passed in the year 1928 and an amendment passed thereto in the following year to increase the rate of interest that particular company was entitled to charge.

I cannot hear my hon.
friend. Before proceeding to deal with the actual terms of the bill, in view of the gratuitously insulting remark offered me by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) I feel constrained to advise hon.
members of this house that I have not any interest of any nature or kind, professional or financial, in this bill. I sponsored the bill merely at the request of a fellow practitioner, the Ottawa agent of the solicitor for this particular company. That, Mr. Speaker, is the only connection I have with the bill.
To illustrate to this house the . extent to which some hon. gentlemen have gone in opposing the bill, I would ask hon. members to recall the argument made the other night by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill). He dilated at great length upon section 8 and endeavoured to make it appear that because the section provided that certain sections of the Loan Companies Act were not applicable to this company, therefore this company was being given some special pivilege or special concession. Nothing could be more misleading. Do not misunderstand me. I do not allege that the hon. gentleman deliberately misled the house; I think rather his statement was made in ignorance of the Loan Companies Act, because every single section of that act which by section 8 of this bill is not made applicable to this particular company confers some special privileges upon companies to whom that act applies. And so the effect of section 8 is not to amplify the powers of this particular company, but to take from it some of the powers which may be exercised by any loan company.

subtopic: SERVICE LOAN AND FINANCE CORPORATION
speechtext: Does that apply to the other acts that I also mentioned, a large number of the sections of which are eliminated?

subtopic: SERVICE LOAN AND FINANCE CORPORATION
speechtext:
I will deal with them in a moment; I am taking one part of his speech at a time. Then my hon. friend from Battle River (Mr. Spencer) had a special theme for the speech which he delivered in opposition to the bill. I ask hon. members to recall the number of times that that hon. gentleman has stood in his place and related to those of us who were within hearing the terrrible atrocities that were being perpetrated by the banks upon the farmers of western Canada. How well do we recollect his telling us that in spite of the ample security which his constituents had to offer, the banks would not make them loans. How often have I lent a sympathetic ear to him and to his colleagues in their appeal for the establishment of an intermediate credit institution because the banks were utterly failing to meet the credit situation in this country, particularly in the western provinces. In view of these statements made by the hon. member, I would ask the house to listen to

Loan and Finance Corporation
this gem which fell from his lips the other night as the theme of his speech, when he said:
If anyone wanting to borrow money has any security at all to offer and is a good risk, our present banking facilities are available.
Then my hon. friend from Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) appeared to work himself into a state of frenzy over the fact that although this bill provides that notwithstanding anything contained in the Interest Act, or in the Money Lenders Act, or in paragraph (c) of the. Loan Companies Act, and that in certain hypothetical circumstances which were stated to the superintendent of insurance, he answered to the effect that in such a hypothetical case, but one not likely to occur in actual practice, it would be possible for the total charges for interest, services, collections, and so on, in the event of the debtor defaulting, to amount to the equivalent of 17 per cent interest. Let me ask my hon. friend if he has read the provisions of the Interest Act? I would call his attention to section 2:
Except as otherwise provided by this or by any other act of the parliament of Canada, any person may stipulate for, allow and exact on any contract .or agreement whatsoever any rate of interest or of discount which is agreed upon.
That is one of the provisions which would be beneficial to this company if it had as its objective the exacting of usurious rates as alleged by my hon. friend. But that power is taken away from the company by this bill.
Now, Mr. Speaker, let me be very frank and say to the house that this bill has as its objects of incorporation: (1) to permit the acquisition by this dominion company, what is in effect an amalgamation, of two provincial corporations now carrying on business in the province of Ontario; (2) to overcome the provision of the Money Lenders Act which stipulates that on loans of less than $500 a certain limitation is put upon the charges wihch may be imposed for interest, and so on. I make that statement very frankly. This bill proposes that in substitution for that provision there shall be imposed upon this company the several limitations which are set out in the bill, including government inspection of its operations by the superintendent of insurance. May I ask hon. members to bear in mind that, subject to the provision of the Money Lenders Act which I have outlined, individuals may on loans in excess of S500 charge any rate of interest that they may desire provided it is stipulated in writing; but by this bill this company is restrained from exercising that privilege. By the way, that provision in the Interest Act has no relation to real estate mortgages.

Again I come back to another point raised by my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni. He seemed to think that it was a terribly iniquitous thing that the rate of interest prescribed by this bill should be allowed by way of discount on the amount loaned. May I point out to him that for years and years and years money has been borrowed and loaned on second mortgages, and many of us- including myself-have been glad to borrow money on second mortgage and accept from 20 to 25 per cent less than the face value of the mortgage, repaying the principal by quarterly instalments spread over a period of five years, and paying interest, not upon the actual amount advanced but upon the amount specified in the mortgage deed. There has not been any great howl or any loud complaint, so far as I have heard, from those who have raised money by way of second mortgage, or from those builders who discount their second mortgages in order to get capital with which to continue their operations.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I point out that this bill is in almost the exact terms of bills incorporating other companies. If my hon. friends feel that there are not sufficient safeguards in the bill to protect the interests of the public who may wish to deal with this company surely the proper course is to raise these objections before the banking and commerce committee; let us amend the bill so that it will protect the public, if protection is required, and do not let us capriciously refuse this company incorporation.
My hon. friends have made a great deal of the fact that before the banking and commerce committee the superintendent of insurance said, in reply to a hypothetical question, that it might be possible for this company to collect an amount which would be equivalent to 16 per cent or 17 per cent interest. I think in fairness to this house those hon. gentlemen should have advised the house that the superintendent of insurance approved of this bill; that the superintendent of insurance advised the committee that two similar companies were already operating, that his inspection of one company disclosed that it had on loan some $600,000 but up to date had not paid one cent of profit to the shareholders, because none was available; that the superintendent of insurance said that from his inspection he found everything in order and that the department had not received a single complaint from any person.
I am quite free to confess that there may be those holding the view that it is not in the public interest to encourage the borrowing of

Privilege-Mr. Neill
money by those who have not such securities to offer as would be accepted by banks or loan companies, but it must be remembered that, under the Loan Companies Act, loan companies can loan only up to sixty per cent of the value of the security offered. To those hon. members who hold this view I do not attempt to advance an argument in favour of this bill, except to say this: If other similar companies are in operation; if they have been successful in meeting a public need; if there has not been public complaint, why discriminate against this particular bill?

This bill bears every resemblance to a sign I have seen hanging in front of some offices in the larger cities, consisting of three brass (balls. The farmers of western Canada do not want to pay 17 per cent; they do not want to have chattel mortgages or other indebtedness, and I cannot understand the hon. member sponsoring a bill of this kind. I wonder why the hon. member did not state what would be the fee for drawing the documents in connection with the loan of money.

I remember in the pioneer days paying 20 per cent for the loan of money from the same sort of outfit, and we struggled and worked to get out of the clutches of those people We will not have them back on the prairies if I have any say as a member of parliament.
I am not going to take up very much of the time of the house. I was very glad indeed to hear the statement of the hon. member for West York (Mr. Lawson) to-night, although I am sure it was not necessary for him to explain to the house that he had no personal interest in the bill. I am quite sure we all know that he is only performing his duty as a member of this house in bringing forward this measure for consideration; there is no question of anything else in my mind.
I would submit, however, that he has failed to give a really sound reason why this bill should be recommitted. In the select standing committee very careful consideration was given this measure; we had all the provisions explained in detail, and my hon. friend did not throw any additional light on the bill by his remarks to-night. He told us we should send this bill back to the committee, but he did not say on what grounds that should be done. Does he mean to infer that the consideration given this bill previously was not careful consideration? Does he mean to suggest that the committee was remiss in its duty, that it did not go into all the details, that it did not understand the principle involved in the bill? Or does he mean to suggest that if he had been present he could have thrown more light on the matter and presented the bill in better form and in a more eloquent way? He did not even say that; if he had made that argument at least it would have been one reason why we should recommit the bill, but there is no suggestion of any amendment to the bill; there is no charge that we failed to consider it adequately; there is no argument offered why it should go back. We are only told that my hon. friend would like it to go back. I should very much like to please him; he is very genial and is an excellent colleague in this house, but I should like some reason for an action of this kind. While I appreciate the splendid presentation he made to-night; while I appreciate his erudition and knowledge of the laws which are involved, I was disappointed in that he failed to give us a real reason why we should recommit the bill.

I
rise to a question of privilege before we proceed with the discussion; I think a matter of privilege is always in order. Yesterday
Privilege-Mr. Neill

afternoon I made a statement in this house which was later contradicted by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett). I have in my hand proof that I was right, and I wish to clear up the matter now. I will require to read only a couple of sentences. At page 3947 of Hansard, I said:
I am rather surprised that the Prime Minister has announced what really is a very important departure of policy at this late stage, and in a rather casual way, connected with a bill that does not immediately refer to that matter.

Preambles to bills are
not policies; surely the hon. member knows that. This is not a matter of privilege at all.

The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Chaplin for concurrence in the third and final report of the select standing committee on railways and shipping, owned, operated and controlled by the government.

I
feel I cannot allow this opportunity to pass without once more making a plea to the now quite genial Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) and the often genial Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) for the construction of the Peace River outlet at the earliest possible moment. It may not be amiss at this stage briefly to review the history of this proposal.
It is some seventeen years since the agitation began for a Peace River outlet. Nine years ago in this house, and again in 1923, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy) moved resolutions asking for the con-

struction of the outlet. The persistent efforts of the settlers in that territory were apparently without avail. In both years, 1922 and 1923, the pioneers of that country sent down to Ottawa at their own expense delegations to interview the then government. Nothing was done. As a result of the agitation by my hon. friend from Peace River the house in
1922 voted the sum of $50,000 for a reconnaissance survey. This sum of money was, of course, wholly inadequate to undertake any comprehensive survey of the passes out of the Peace River district to Vancouver, and in
1923	it was found necessary to vote a further
sum of $75,000. With this vote a fairly complete survey was made of a route between Aggie, on the Edmonton Dunvegan line, about 200 miles northwest of Edmonton, and Obed, a point 200 miles west of Edmonton. Following this, and early in 1924, a meeting was held at the office of the then Minister of Railways, the Hon. George P. Graham, to discuss the whole question. There were present at that meeting the following gentlemen:	Sir Henry Thornton, Mr. E.
W. Beatty, president of the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Hon. Herbert Greenfield, then premier of Alberta, the Hon. Vernon Smith, Minister of Railways and Telephones in the Alberta government, Mr. W. F. Maclean, M.P., Conservative member for Toronto, Mr. D. M. Kennedy, M.P., and the Hon. John Oliver, premier of British Columbia. As a result of that meeting it was agreed that the two railways, the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific, should get together and undertake an examination into the available routes out of the Peace. This was done, and the report made to the Minister of Railways was tabled in the house in 1926. This report, an important one at that stage, was signed by five engineers, two of them representing the Canadian National Railways and three representing the Canadan Pacific. The report recommended the Obed route as the best, after an examination of the Peace pass, the Pine pass, and the Monkman pass routes. In the year 1924 the Prime Minister, the present leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), made a tour of western Canada.
Where was that meeting held?

In the office of the Minister of Railways. In 1924 the then Prime Minister made a tour of western Canada, and speaking in the Presbyterian church in Edmonton-an estimable place in which to make definite promises-he pledged himself in

Railways and Shipping Report
such a decided way that headlines appeared in the following day's paper like these:
King pledges self to the Peace River cause. Premier promises outlet to Pacific just as soon as humanly possible. Railway will be built, declares Prime Minister at a mass meeting here. Government has but minority in Commons; says times are now difficult and everybody must have a little patience, but Liberal party is not falling down on any of its pledges.
I do not wish unnecessarily to remind lion, gentlemen of promises they have made, but I want to place before the house the fact that both political parties in this country are definitely and irrevocably pledged to the construction of the Peace River outlet. That is my sole object in referring to this promise. I quote from the speech made by the then Prime Minister:
There is to the north of this city a great tract of land that is crying out for development. The Peace River country is amongst the richest in Canada

That statement has been more than borne out by the experience of the years that have passed.
-but before the proper development of that country can take place an outlet to the Pacific coast is an absolute necessity. I pledge myself-
That reminds me of the manner in which the pledges of the present Prime Minister were made.
I pledge myself that as soon as it is humanly possible the great Peace River country will be given that measure of railway relief that will bring to the pioneers of that country the outlet they have been so long denied, and will open up the country for prospective settlers. I must, however, sound the same note to you here as I did to the citizens of Saskatoon. The times that we are passing through are very difficult, and I would ask you to have a little patience, and in as short a time as possible a railway outlet will be provided for Peace River and northern Alberta districts that will open up an era of prosperity for that province which will not be equalled by any other province in Canada.
At this stage I submit this thought, which I will develop later, that the time to undertake great public projects of this kind is not in a period of prosperity but in a time of adversity. At that time we were passing through one of those minor depressions, and the Prime Minister of the day used that depression as an excuse for avoiding the work. The country steadily emerged from that period of depression into what was described by the Liberal party then, as it has been described since, as the greatest era of prosperity that Canada had ever seen. The Minister of Finance of the late government was wont to talk in this house fervently of the buoyant
revenues of the country, of our expanding foreign trade, of the tremendous development of transportation, of the increased production of goods in Canada. Yet no Peace River outlet was constructed. It could not be constructed in bad times, it was said, and it was not constructed in a prosperous period.
Now, that I may link up the other part of the project with this, may I submit to the house a statement made by the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen in parliament, following that declaration of the present leader of the opposition. On October 1, Mr. Meighen, speaking also in Edmonton, said:
I have always urged that the north country should have railway relief. I cannot be accused of making futile promises such as the Hon. Mackenzie King promised in the speech from the throne at the opening of the last session of parliament when he stated that he was going to give railway relief to the north country, and nothing has been done.
No; but if Mr. Meighen and his party were elected it was to be one of their first undertakings. The report of the five engineers to which I referred a moment ago was tabled in the house in 1926. As hon. members will recollect, 1926 was the year of that hectic and stormy session when no one knew what the government to-morrow was likely to be. It was the hectic session of the Customs scandal, during which two governments went down to defeat. During that session a proposal was made in the house, though never acted upon, that instead of constructing an outlet, a rate ought to be struck on the basis of mileage- the mileage of a direct outlet instead of the actual mileage by Edmonton. Nothing, however, was done in this connection. In the following session of 1927, the hon. member for Peace River moved the following motion:
That, in the opinion of this house, the time has arrived for the commencement forthwith and the completion in the near future of a direct railway outlet from the Peace River country to the Pacific coast.
That motion, which was in keeping with the definite pledges made by both the Liberal and Conservative parties of that day, was resisted in this house. Hon. Mr. Dunning, then Minister of Railways and Canals, objected to it and it was referred to the committee on railways and canals, along with the report of the five engineers. During the investigation held before that committee it was found on examination of the report that the Obed route was the only route of the four routes possible of which a complete survey had been undertaken and that the reports in connection with the Peace and Monkman passes



Railways and Shipping Report
were mere guesswork. The committee then brought in what amounted to an innocuous recommendation to the effect that a continuous study of the development of the Peace River district and the outlets should be carried on. To the motion for concurrence in that report the hon. member for Peace River moved an amendment calling for an immediate and complete survey of those passes which had not yet been surveyed, namely, the Peace, the Monkman and the Pine passes. The vote on the amendment was 87 for and 97 against. The then Minister of Railways promised that in any case the government would ask the Canadian National Railways to complete the surveys to a stage where they would have sufficient information to be able to say, when it was determined to build the line: This is the territory through which it should pass.
Mr. Murray Hill, of the Canadian National Railways, was sent out through the mountains in 1928. He made a complete survey of the approach to the Peace pass from the north side of the Peace river and between the Peace river and Dunvegan. Mr. Murray Hill who is an estimable engineer possessing quite a reputation reported definitely against the Peace pass route and recommended that further surveys be undertaken to show how impossible that route was. It happens that the crossing at Beatton river and the approach to the canyon at Hudson's Hope along the banks of the Peace river is made at a point where there are exceedingly steep banks which slide during times of rain. At this point I would like to direct attention to the last paragraph of Mr. Murray Hill's report, which reads as follows:
The Peace pass seems to be the most favoured. To my knowledge, there have not been any lines run through this route, either on the north or south side of the Peace river. I would therefore suggest that these surveys be made in order that definite information may be available to show the difficulties in construction and operation of lines over these routes. The Obed route, from information available, is unquestionably the best Pacific outlet for the Peace River country as a whole. It is, however, unpopular with certain sections of the country. Actual surveys have been made over this route and also the Pine pass route. In order that a correct comparison may be made between all routes, surveys must be made over the other two, viz: Monkman pass and Peace pass routes.
Who was that?

Mr. Murray Hill of the Canadian National Railways. Up to this Stage the principal objection to the construction of the outlet seems to have been that there was not sufficient information avail-

able to justify the selection of any definite pass through which the line should run. During the debates in this house it became apparent that both the government and the railways were reluctant to undertake the construction of this outlet because of the position in which they found the northern railways of the province of Alberta. This was apparently the chief stumbling block in the way of definite and immediate action. Both Alberta and British Columbia were directly interested. British 'Columbia owned the famous Pacific Great Eastern Railway and whatever route might be selected might affect the business of that line as well has have an effect upon the political and economic life of the province. That province as well as Alberta was directly interested in whatever route might be selected. The objection in connection with the ownership and operation of the railways in northern Alberta has now been removed.
Before I continue may I mention that the Minister of Railways of that day, the Hon. Mr. Dunning, referred to the Alberta railways and the Pacific Great Eastern railway as being white elephants and suggested that one of the reasons for difficulty in settling this matter was that the premiers of Alberta and British Columbia were doing theiir best to slough off these white elephants on the Canadian National Railways. Mr. Dunning, on one occasion, called attention to the fact that the provinces were unable to pay the cost of operation of their railways. I am afraid that Mr. Dunning was sadly mistaken in his facts, because the first year of operation by the province of the Edmonton, Dunvegan and British Columbia Railway showed an operating surplus of $300,000, while the second year s operation showed a surplus of $800,000, sufficient to pay the fixed charges on the replacement value of the railway.
What year was that?

I am not
certain of the exact year, but I think it was 1928.
Did that amount not include a certain amount paid by the two railways?

The report of the Department of Railways and Telephones of our province is as I have stated, that the operating surplus for 1928 was about $800,000, which would cover the fixed charges on the replacement value of the line. The government and people of Alberta were positively astounded at the successful outcome of government ownership.

Railways and Shipping Report
Mr. MA.NION:	Last year the operating
surplus included an amount of about SI,000,000, or perhaps $2,000,000, which had been paid in by the two railways and which was taken in as operating revenue.

I am speaking of the period when these lines were operated by the provincial government and not by the two railways.
We now reach the stage where the second objection to the construction of the Peace river outlet had been removed. The railways were sold to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company for $26,000,000, on the understanding that up until December 31, 1928, an offer would be open to the Canadian National Railways to share fifty-fifty in the purchase of these lines. This offer was accepted and to-day the 'lines in northern Alberta are operated jointly by the Canadian Pacific and Canadian National railways.
Previous to 1927 the Edmonton, Dunvegan and British Columbia Railway had been operated by the Canadian Pacific Railway. I am afraid that the showings reported by the Canadian Pacific Railway were not a3 favourable as those shown when the lines were operated by the government. In spite of this fact, both the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National attempted to secure a lease of the roads for five or ten years. For reasons best known to the province of Alberta, this lease was refused and the lines were operated by the government, and then the classic agreement was made with the Canadian National Railways. I mention this only in order to introduce this statement:	It was during the negotiations for
the transfer of these northern lines that Sir Henry Thornton in a letter to Premier Greenfield of Alberta stated that he would be prepared to recommend the construction of this outlet to the Pacific coast when the Peace River district had developed an export of grain amounting to ten million bushels a year, or equivalent tonnage, for three years. I now wish to give to the house information as to the tonnage shipped out of that district.

It was a
straight offer-when ten million bushels of grain had been produced.
Or equivalent tonnage.

There was
no mention of that; it was ten million bushels of grain.

I think the hon. gentleman is mistaken.
22110-255J
No; I have seen the letter.	[DOT]

So did we
see the letter. Mr. Greenfield, as premier, had it at the time. But it does not matter which of us is correct because the fact is that that district has exceeded the requirements of Sir Henry Thornton as set forth in his letter, whether he said ten million bushels or equivalent tonnage. It is intensely interesting to notice the growth of the development of that territory. In 1925 they shipped out 89,000 tons of grain or 5,300,000 bushels; in 1926, 6,000,000 bushels; 1927, 6,331,765 bushels; in 1928, 11,506,000 bushels; 1929, 7,323,000 bushels; 1930, 11,050,000 bushels; 1931, up to April 30, 10,067,000 bushels. It therefore must be clear to anybody who examines the facts that the requirements set up by Sir Henry Thornton have been more than met and that the tonnage of that district fully justifies the construction of this line. This year, may I remind the house, in all western Canada, covered as it is almost like a blanket with depression, the one really bright spot is the Peace River territory, There the prospects for a crop are still good. The prospects are that the tonnage there this year will equal if not exceed last year's tonnage, but that will depend, of course, upon weather conditions from now on.
This northern district in our province has shown a better return in railway revenue during the last few years than any other district I know of in all of Canada. In 1929 the Northern Alberta Railways showed operating revenues of $2,232,156, and in 1930, $2,253,737. The net revenues will perhaps be more interesting and comprehensive. The net revenue in 1929 was over three-quarters of a million dollars, $795,000, and in 1930, $301,000. In that year hon. members will recall we had a small crop over quite an extensive area in the west.
In the following session of 1930 the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy) endeavoured to secure the ear of the house for the construction of the outlet and moved a motion on going into supply-a want of confidence motion it has sometimes been described. On that occasion the government accepted the motion, and, as was pointed out, technically defeated themselves. In the course of that debate the then Prime Minister, now the leader of the opposition, said on May 5, 1930, as reported in Hansard of that date at page 1809:
We all-

I venture to say they ought to be, and if they are not I will give ample reasons why this government should be ready to advance as a loan the moneys necessary to construct their share o>f the road. Up in that great territory there is a magnet drawing the poor unfortunates who are left destitute on the dried out prairies of southern Saskatchewan and Alberta. In this month of July arrangements have been made for the transportation of a great many settlers from the southern portion of the prairie provinces into the Peace River district. Those men are not drifting into the cities and joining the ranks of the unemployed so that they may eventually become charges upon the state. They are doing their best to make another start. The persistence of such people has helped to make Canada what it is, and their action would justify this government undertaking to give them some assistance Iby the construction of the outlet. I repeat that if the 1931 crop comes up to the estimates made by the bureau of statistics and by those who reside in the territory in question there will not be any serious loss in this year's movement of grains and commodities from that territory. The settlers up there however are labouring under a serious handicap. They went in with courage in their hearts to tear out a home from the wilderness. They have been fighting for from seventeen to twenty years under a freight handicap the seriousness of which few people in eastern Canada can appreciate. The cost of moving their grain to Vancouver via Edmonton is 5, 6 or 7 cents higher than the cost of moving it from Edmonton to Vancouver. Yet a line of railway could be constructed which would put those people in as close proximity to Vancouver as the people in Edmonton are to-day. The line would have the effect of building up a great territory and would give those people heart and head to keep on fighting to build up their country.
May I point out that the money will be spent anyway, because money must be spent to relieve unemployment in Canada. Why dole it out to single men or unfortunate married men through relief measures when useful work can be provided? Here is an opportunity. Turn all the unemployed in the country to the task of constructing a useful financial asset, one which will be of great benefit to the western section of Canada. Such a line would be beneficial to the province of British Columbia as much as to the province of Alberta. No better suggestion could be advanced than that in this great day of need on the part of hundreds of thousands of people throughout Canada a few thousand could be used to undertake forthwith the construction of this line. Time would be required for its completion. I hope however that the present government will not wait until the dying days of their regime four years hence to make more promises such as the Prime Minister has made and such as were outlined in the Conservative platform at the Winnipeg convention. Here is the chance for the present administration to justify its existence and formulate a real, constructive government policy in connection with this matter.
