MANION (Minister of Railways and Canals) r I have been listening this afternoon and this evening to the debate on the motion of the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) for concurrence in the report of the railways and shipping committee. At this late hour I have no intention of taking up much of the time of the house. Not only is the hour late but we have reached a late stage in the session; therefore my remarks will be brief.
As I listened to the debate this afternoon the one point which struck me was that it has been of the finest type. Throughout the whole debate there has been practically no political controversy; the whole discussion has been on a high plane, and I feel that the

house deserves some credit. Following the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) so far as I could see adopted a similar attitude in every respect. The use of three expressions struck me particularly. He said that when they came into power they desired that the government railways should be given a fair chance, that the management and directorate should be given a free hand, and that politics should not be permitted to enter into such management. I have no thought of injecting into a debate which has been of so pleasant a character anything of a controversial nature, and in regard to those expressions by the right hon. leader of the opposition I could say only that they are ideals which all true Canadians should have m dealing with the Canadian National Railways. I think therefore all hon. members can agree with the ideals and principles upheld by him this afternoon. We can agree that so far as the management of the Canadian National Railways, and, for that matter, any other Canadian railways, is concerned, politics ought to be taboo.
When we realize that to-day we have in the Canadian National Railways a responsibility amounting to over $2,200,000,000 made up of loans, interest, appropriations, and guarantees we realize that the railways are of such vital importance to us and we realize why hon. members are justified in debating the matter in a non-controversial and nonpolitical way; because actually I think our whole economic structure depends upon the successful solution of the railway problems of Canada.
The discussion to-day was on the report of the special railway committee, a report which was brought into this house unanimously by the members of the committee in the absence of only one of those originally appointed. May I at this moment do what I fear no one else has done-although I have no doubt it was an oversight-congratulate the chairman of that committee, the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin), on the excellent work which he did, particularly in bringing down a unanimous report with the constructive criticisms contained therein.
Hear, hear.

I am glad to hear applause from the other side, because I know hon. members opposite agree with the report, as of course do our friends on this side. It was not an easy matter for the hon. member for Lincoln to bring about that happy result. I was present at most of the meetings. He had to hold a number of meetings, he had to submit various reports to the members,

and, as the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) pointed out this afternoon, there are suggestions in this report that had to be accepted in a spirit of compromise. But after all, the spirit of our democratic institutions is a spirit of compromise; for I do not suppose you could get twenty-two members of this house to agree on the same ideas or the same ideals. So it is all the more to the credit of the hon. member for Lincoln that he finally succeeded in getting twenty-one members of the committee to sign the report and to agree on the constructive criticisms embodied therein. While listening to the debate this evening I looked over the membership of the committee and find that ten of them are from the opposite side of the house and eleven from this side, which indicates a very good division of the committee from the political standpoint, and emphasizes the excellent work which was done by the chairman in bringing about that unanimity of view. All opinions were expressed, because I have no doubt that while my hon. friend from North Waterloo-who has been in this house about the same number of years as I have- has been a persistent and consistent champion of public ownership, there are other members of the committee who have been just as strong in favour of private ownership. All parties were represented:	the
Liberal party, the Conservative party, the Progressive party and the Labour party in the person of the member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps).
This afternoon not only the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) and my right hon. friend the leader of the government (Mr. Bennett), but my hon. friend from North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) and my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), who was not a member of the committee-all of those and others as well supported in a general way, in fact almost in toto, the report. I was particularly glad to have the support of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre because after all-and I say this in no spirit of criticism- he does not too often agree with other members on questions of this sort, and I think his endorsation of the report was perhaps the best praise that could be bestowed upon it.
My hon. friend from Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) took an attitude with regard to the report which I think was hardly justified. He stated, in effect, that the report was futile and that the committee also was futile. I do not agree with his criticism. For the first time so far as I can remember in the history of these committees this year's
committee brought in a report which, although critical, is constructively critical, and instead of merely handing back the accounts as submitted to them, the committee has suggested useful changes that might be made by the management of the railroad in order the better to establish the system on a basis of economic success.
May I say in this regard that while the discussion was proceeding this afternoon one of these suggestions was put into effect by the directors themselves. The directors hold their meetings on the third Tuesday of every month, and at their meeting to-day in the city of Montreal I was informed they were going to discuss and deal with this report. While this debate has been in progress I have received a telegram from Sir Henry Thornton which may be of interest to the house. He wires:
That the board this afternoon passed the following resolution:
Resolved that all officers and employees, excepting those whose rates of pay and working conditions are governed by scheduled agreements, earning in excess of $3,600 per annum shall be reduced by 10 per cent for a period of 10 months from the first of August, 1931. At the expiration of this period the deductions herein included shall be restored unless the board otherwise orders.
Be it further resolved that no salary in excess of $3,600 per annum shall by virtue of such deduction be reduced below $3,600.
That action is along the lines of the course taken by the Canadian Pacific Railway management a couple of months ago when they reduced the salaries of their executives by 10 per cent. I do not know how far down the line they went; perhaps the reductions went further than those mentioned in this telegram, but at any rate it was stated that by this means the Canadian Pacific Railway would save some millions of dollars. That action this afternoon by the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways seems at least suggestive in view of the clauses of the report which I shall now read. I hold in my hand Votes and Proceedings for last Thursday, in which the report of the special committee was printed. These are the three clauses which I desire to quote:
Certain questions relating to the salaries and emoluments paid to executive officers of the company were asked by members of the committee, and were by resolution of the committee submitted to a subcommittee for consideration.	.
Your committee while of opinion that many of the salaries are much too generous, and in some instances excessive, accede to the expressed wish of the president that the list be not published for the reasons given by him.

A little further down in the report will be found the following:
In view of the decreased revenues of the company, and the economies being made in other branches of the service, your committee are of opinion that the executive committee of the board of directors should immediately consider the whole question of salaries, allowances, disbursements, pensions and retirement provisions for executive officers and officials of the company, receiving salaries of $5,000 and over in order that every reasonable and proper economy should be effected.
So that the board of directors this afternoon went a step further even than the committee had requested them to go.
May I say to my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre, who spoke this afternoon commending in a general way the whole report, that this does not affect the wages of those of whom he spoke. This affects the executive officers, from my reading of Sir Henry Thornton's telegram; it does not affect the ordinary wage earner, the day labourer, the piece job man or the running trades; it does not affect the ordinary workingman on the road up, we will say, to conductors, brake-men, engineers, and so on. I doubt if it at all affects the operating staff of the road, but rather the executive staff as was suggested by the committee which dealt with this matter. So it appears to me as though that committee, if it did not inspire the action of the board of directors, at least supported it inasmuch as it antedated their action by a few days.
So I repeat that to my mind this is a very useful report in its constructive criticisms and suggestions with regard to the national road. I say this in no spirit of criticism, but I think perhaps it is a pity that in past years the committee did not act in a similar way and offer constructive criticisms. I am indirectly criticizing myself, because for some years, at least, while sitting on the opposition side of the house I was a member of that committee. I think this report generally is constructive; it is not perfect, but it is a real effort to be helpful in the work of the road.
Now for a moment or two I wish to deal with some of the remarks of my hon. friend from North Waterloo, particularly his remarks with regard to the board of directors. Again without desiring to cast reflections may I say that I believe the present board of directors is the best board the Canadian National Railways ever had. Perhaps it is natural that I should make that statement because this government appointed them, but at the same time I believe more than the usual care was taken in these appointments. My hon. friend from North

Waterloo took the attitude, which is taken by many others, that there should be no politics in the appointment of such a board as this. Of course there are arguments against appointments of that kind being political, but so long as we have party government in this country, just so long will the party in power naturally lean towards people who are friendly to it in making appointments of any kind. I think that is no reflection on party government. Not only that, but if my hon. friend from North Waterloo could see some of the letters I received after this directorate were appointed he would not think they were all friends of ours, because there were some very severe criticisms in regard to the political leanings of some of the men who were appointed.
I suppose there were a great many applicants?

Yes, but I am speaking of political criticisms by our friends, some of whom thought we did not pick Conservatives for these positions. But may I say that I do not believe the political affiliations of any member of that board, whether appointed by the Liberals or by the Conservatives, necessarily need lessen the ability of the board, because after all there are outstanding business men in this country who are of Liberal persuasion, as there are outstanding business men who are of Conservative persuasion. It is not difficult, in view of that fact, to choose a good group, as we have done. I do not believe in playing about with words; I will admit that they were largely of our political persuasion, but I still maintain that they are an outstanding group of men.
I will grant this: Probably a smaller board might give better and more efficient management to the railway. Yet this is a government railway, and the difficulty in creating a small board is that you get complaints from all over the country. When my hon. friends were in power I am sure when they made similar appointments they came up against the same type of criticism we have received since those appointments were made. Any appointments to a government institution as this road is to a certain extent though handled by the management, since it is dependent upon the government for the money it may need-will bring about the same criticism. So long as this is a government road we will get demands from different portions of the country that they be represented, and from different classes in the country that they be represented. For example, when hon.

gentlemen opposite were in power, they appointed Tom Moore as representing Labour. We replaced him and a number of others who were formerly on the board.
You did not replace him; you reappointed him.

I meant to say we reappointed him to the board. We have had demands from the agricultural sections of the country; I have received many personally; some were read by my hon. friend from South Perth (Mr. Sanderson) some time ago, and others have been forwarded by supporters of the party on this side of the house, asking that agriculture be represented in the same way. So long as we have this road as more or less of a government institution we will have these demands that certain portions or certain classes of the country be represented. That is an advantage which a company such as the Canadian Pacific Railway has over a government institution such as the Canadian National Railways. They are not forced to consider the geography of the country, as my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) put it; they are not forced to consider different classes. They are in the position-the happy position, if you like-of being able to appoint those men whom they see fit to appoint from a straight business and executive standpoint. While I was sitting here I looked up the board of directors of the Canadian Pacific Railway; I had it in mind, and just checked it up. I find that they have exactly the same number of directors on the board; they have seventeen, and of those directors nine come from Montreal, two from London, one from New York-and what complaints we would receive if we should appoint a New York director on the Canadian National-one from Brantford, one from Oshawa, one from Winnipeg, one from Vancouver, and one from Toronto. Only four provinces are represented on that board, but the Canadian Pacific Railway have that advantage in that they are not forced to satisfy the different geographical or political sections of this country as a government road is forced to do to a certain extent.
Let me give an illustration of what I have been saying. When we appointed this board the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta were not represented-and were not represented on the previous board-and we had the very strongest protests conceivable from those provinces because of that fact. I presume the same thing occurred when hon. gentlemen opposite were in office. In a short time we
intend to appoint two directors from those provinces, so that every province will be represented.
It may be of interest to the house to know the size of the boards of directors of some important companies in Canada. None of them is small. The directors of the Bank of Montreal number 21; of the Bank of Nova Scotia, 20; of the Bank of Commerce, 37, and of the Royal bank, 28. Of course many of those boards were enlarged because of the amalgamation of different banks, but the fact remains that these companies have large directorates. There are 17 directors of the Sun Life Assurance Company; of International Nickle-and I presume a great many hon. members here remember International Nickle -there are 25 directors, and the board of directors of the Bell Telephone Company consists of 15. So it will be apparent that very few of the large companies have a smaller number of directors than the Canadian National Railways.
I will admit, however, that I agree with the hon. member for North Waterloo; probably if we could pick four or five strong men as directors, more efficiency might result. They would have to be situated close to Montreal, at least within a night's run; they would have to be big, powerful men, independent of any smaller considerations, men who would give their very best to making the Canadian National Railways a success from a business standpoint. I believe if you could pick five men like that and give them a better salary, such as has been suggested, and generally put the road in their hands probably you would get better management than you can get from a directorate scattered from the Atlantic to the Pacific, which cannot meet more than once a month. Men in Prince Edward Island, in Vancouver or Victoria, in Calgary or in other places widely separated cannot get east or west to the centre where the meeting is held more often than once a month. That is one of the penalties we pay for having a democracy. No doubt democracy is the best form of government we have eo far encountered, but it has its faults. This is one of the reasons why we have so many political demands upon the railway and so many protests against any change made in the interests of economy. This very morning I think I received half a dozen letters from various sections of the country protesting against some act of the management of the road, of which I knew nothing, some economy which is being practised and which the

management feels must be carried out because of the reduced earnings of the railway.
It may be interesting to the house to know as it is only right the house should know, that the gross earnings of the national railways for the first six months of this year are down some $22,000,000 as compared with the same six months in 1930. In 1930 the total year's earnings were down $46,000,000 as compared with 1929. In view of those figures, and in view of the fact that last year the government of Canada had to meet interest to the public amounting to nearly $30,000,000, which the railways had not earned and which therefore had to be paid on behalf of the people, it is, I think, realizable that the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway-because that railway also has been affected-must of necessity economize. It is not quite fair, therefore, on the part of people in various sections of Canada to take the attitude that economies may be made, but not in their particular districts. And that, I am afraid, is the attitude which is taken in every part of the Dominion whenever any slight change is made by the Canadian National Railways or the Canadian Pacific- for I get protests sometimes in regard to the economies practised by the Canadian Pacific as well. I do not think it is reasonable, in view of the situation as I have indicated it, that people should protest as vociferously as they do.
My remarks so far have been quite general, and I wish now to discuss one or two particular questions. Let me for a moment or two consider the Peace River outlet. He has been very persistent, I will not say obstinate, in his presentation of the case, and as a result of his efforts he has obtained altogether 135 or 140 returns. That, I think, is a record in the whole history of parliamentary institutions in Canada, though I fancy it is a rather doubtful record. Now, in justice to the government, I would point out that last year the Canadian National Railways planned $8,000,000 worth of additions and betterments which were not carried out, so that Riviere du Loup constituted but one-hundredth part of the additions and better-

ments which had been contemplated but could not be realized. The Canadian National Railways took the attitude, with respect to most of these additions and improvements, that in view of the decreased earnings of the system such undertakings must be restricted. I agree with my right hon. friend from Argenteuil (Sir George Perley), who in reply to the member for Temiscouata, spoke this afternoon, and I accept entirely the statement that this was a government re-sponsiblity. No hon. member has any right whatever to lay any undue blame upon him, as the hon. member for Temiscouata has done, because he was but one member of the government. I take my full share of responsibility for the action taken in regard to this matter, and I submit that it is not fair that my colleague from Argenteuil should be blamed, if there is to be any blame at all, more than the rest of the government. In regard to the Peace River outlet, the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) made a vigorous speech in behalf of this cause. I have sat in the house a few years and I have heard eloquent speeches made by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy), by the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Fraser), and by the hon. member for Bow River. These three gentlemen-I will not particularize-have been strong and persistent advocates of an outlet to be built from the Peace River territory. I do not mind telling them frankly that I sympathize with them in this regard, although, so far as I remember, I have never made a speech anywhere dealing with this subject. I have not made any promises on the matter. But having lived all my younger days in a pioneer section of the country, in northern Ontario, where transportation was not easy and where we were largely isolated from other parts of Canada, I can sympathize with these hon. gentlemen who feel so strongly on the need for an outlet from that vast territory. May I point out, however, that the solution is not quite so easy as was suggested by my hon.

friend from Bow River in his otherwise excellent speech. The hon. gentleman spoke as though it were only a matter of the government stepping in and building this immense project. He spoke as though the two railways had come to a decision as to what they wanted and it would be a simple matter for the government to raise the $40,000,000 with which to construct the outlet forthwith. The fact of the matter is, the railways have not come to any decision. It is true that the route referred to by the hon. gentleman, the Aggie-Obed route, was one of the early suggestions of the Canadian National Railways But the Canadian Pacific Railway has submitted a report recently in which they take exception to that suggested route; they suggest a different one from the route proposed by the Canadian National Railways. And then there are other routes which have been proposed. For instance, there is the suggestion that the present route be maintained, bringing all grain from the Peace River section back towards Edmonton

a backhaul- and taking it towards Vancouver, leaving the route as at present, and putting lower rates into effect. Secondly, there is the Obed route, of which the hon. member for Bow River has spoken. Then there are the Monk-man pass and, the Pine pass, and the Peace pass routes. As a theorist I have studied the situation on the map, have looked into the various reports, and have endeavoured to familiarize myself with the subject. And in a general way I think I have done so. Moreover, I trust that during this summer I shall have the pleasure of a visit to the district. But I submit that it is only fair to say that before the government takes any action in the matter the railways themselves should at least agree to something definite. The hon. member spoke as if the Canadian Pacific Railway at least was ready to build one of these routes at once. I submit that it is not so. I had a conference only last Friday in my office with the heads of the two railways, and they did not propose to put up the money. I do not think I am betraying their confidence when I say that it is the opinion of the two railways at the present time that if this outlet is to be built it should be built by the Canadian government and not by either of the systems. Obviously, therefore, there are a number of questions to be settled before a final decision can be arrived at. Certainly I am of the opinion-and I am sure that in this regard the whole house will agree with me, including the hon. member for Peace River, the hon. member for Cariboo and the hon. member for Bow River-that
we should not undertake in this country the construction of very costly lines of railway which will duplicate the mistakes of the past, without a proper investigation into the whole situation and an endeavour to avoid any such condition. After all, it is far better to have the two railways agreed upon one specific route and to have the government cooperating with them. Surely it is better to have the whole plan carefully laid out than to take chances, undertaking the construction of a road which has not been decided upon by agreement-one railway engineer taking one view and another suggesting something different.
I am interested in the whole question; I am sympathetic to the idea. But at the present time I think it would be unfair to the people of the country at large, and unfair to that section itself, if my right hon. leader (Mr. Bennett) were asked to carry into effect some ill-conceived proposal. I submit that my hon. friends from that section of the country will have to have a little more patience. After all, this government has not yet been one year in power, and I am sure that whatever promises may have been made in this regard were certainly not made by my leader, nor were they made by any other member of this government, to the effect that this road would be built within one year. Nor was any such promise made with respect to any of the large projects which the government has been gradually taking up as time has passed.
May I, in closing, make this observation. Parliament realizes that the country to-day is faced with a serious railway problem. Everyone must admit, when you take into account the immense debt of the railways; the vast governmental guarantees; the fact that the interest to the public to-day is well over a million dollars a week, and that this year it looks as if the national railways have not much chance of paying very much of that $50,000,000 odd which is owing to the public- everyone must admit, I say, in view of these facts, that the situation demands general economy, because of its seriousness. That immense sum of money having to be paid by the people of Canada, this house realizes and I believe the people realize the seriousness of the transportation question. At the same time I do not think this matter is a hopeless one nor do I believe this is a time for panic. I believe in the motto which I suggested some time ago, I think in my remarks on the budget, that with care, caution and economy, with prudence and wise general management of the railways, the whole transportation system of

our country will come back once again to a proper basis of progressive prosperity. Surely we Canadians are hopeful for the future of Canada. This country has not been ruined in a couple of years. We have our fields, our forests, our mines, our waterfalls and our virile people, and this country is going to come back into its own. The day for the people of Canada will return and with that day will return prosperity for both railway systems. Both roads will return again to a proper basis of economic progress, and the spirit which has been shown to-day in this house by every hon. member who has spoken is the spirit which will help to bring back prosperity, not only to Canada but to both the Canadian Pacific and Canadian National railways. They will both soon reach that position of progress and prosperity which we all desire to see them attain.

Mr. Speaker, I hope the house will bear with me for a few moments while I emphasize the points raised by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland). I do so not only because of the importance of the subject itself, but also because the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy), who has been an ardent advocate of the Peace river outlet, is suffering from a bad throat and is unable to speak.
First, let me offer my congratulations to the hon. gentleman who acted as chairman of the railway committee. I am sure that all hon. members appreciate the great qualities he exercised in that capacity. I am glad to know that the report of the committee was adopted unanimously, and I anticipate that it will be concurred in unanimously by this house. My words will not be words of criticism of the Canadian National Railways, although there may be room for criticism, nor will they be words of praise.
I want to point out to the government the necessity of undertaking as speedily as possible the building of a Peace River outlet, and I want to emphasize in particular the economic aspect of that undertaking. The hon. member for Bow River has very ably outlined the history of the struggle of the people of the Peace River district for an outlet to the coast. That struggle has been carried on from 1917 up to the present day, during which period many people flocked into that section of the country in the hope and belief that a railroad would be built and that they would find an outlet for their products. It is now known that the tonnage of produce which could be shipped annually from that section of the country will far exceed the fMr. Manian.]
estimates made by leading railway men of this country as being necessary to warrant the building of a road. Moreover both railways have been making surveys during the last eight years, and practically every possible route has been surveyed. There is now in the hands of the government or available to it all the engineering data necessary to enable it to come to a conclusion as to which route should be selected.
While I did not expect that the minister would say that the Peace river outlet would be built, I did hope for a little more encouragement than he gave us in his remarks. We are glad to have the minister's sympathy; I know the people of the Peace River district, will be glad to have it; but they are looking for something more substantial. To express; it in another way, they are looking for sympathy expressed in material form, or materialized sympathy. If I understood the minister correctly, his chief objection to proceeding immediately with the development of this route was that there does not seem to be any agreement between the two railway companies as to which route should be selected. That disagreement might go on forever because these roads being in competition, no one can say how long it will take them to agree as to which route should be selected.

I should have stated that
the suggestion of the two roads was that engineers be appointed, one by each railway company and one by the government, to go into this question. That will probably be carried out in the near future.

That would seem to show
that some action has been taken to break the deadlock and there is hope that in the near future a definite decision will be arrived at as to which route should be adopted. Perhaps a little more progress has been made than was indicated by the speech of the minister. If that arrangement fails to accomplish anything then the government should not wait any longer for a decision to be made by the railway companies. Having, as I said, at its disposal all the data necessary to arrive at a conclusion it should put its own engineers on the job, decide which route should be built, and proceed to build it.
The need for an outlet is great. I do not think I need to recapitulate what the hon. member for Bow River has so eloquently presented to the house. There is no doubt about the fact that the people are there. In 1928 and 1929 there were homesteaded in this district a total of 1,760,000 acres, and to

date about 5,000,000 acres have been taken up with approximately 1,000,000 acres under cultivation. With such a large portion of the population of Canada, if it is desired that it be expressed in that way, in dire need of facilities of this character, there can be no question about the necessity. It must be remembered that the opening up of this district, which is perhaps the most fertile in the Dominion of Canada, will mean virtually the opening up of a new continent.
It was said not so long ago by statesmen of this country that there were two great railway necessities, the Hudson Bay railway and the Peace River outlet. The Hudson Bay railway has been built, and without making any criticism of that road I have no hesitation in saying that the least important has been built first. I do not think there can be any question as to the relative importance of these two routes. All necessary surveys have been made and there should be no doubt as to which route should be chosen for a Peace River outlet. All the engineering information that is required is to hand. The only question is, when is the road to be built?
Let me point out that there is no political issue here, as I understand it, for both political leaders have declared themselves in unequivocal language as being in favour of the development of the Peace River country by providing it with adequate railway facilities. I refer hon. members to the statement of the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) when making his tour in the west as Prime Minister some time prior to the election of 1925. He had this to say in the city of Edmonton in respect of the Peace River outlet:
There is to the north of this city a great tract of land that is crying out for development.
Incidentally, it is still crying:
The Peace River country is amongst the richest in Canada, but before the proper development of that country can take place an outlet to the Pacific coast is an absolute necessity. I pledge myself that as soon as it is humanly possible the great Peace River country will be given that measure of railway relief that will bring to the pioneers of that country the outlet they have been so long denied, and will open up the eounrty for prospective settlers.
That was the statement of the right hon. leader of the opposition when he was Prime Minister. Let me now quote the declaration of the Conservatives in their great Winnipeg convention, which I presume was accepted by their leader and is accepted by the government to-day. Clause 5 of that declaration
says:
We pledge ourselves to the improvement of the whole scheme of Canadian transportation northward by the completion of the Hudson bay route, and the construction of such branches as may be necessary to render it most readily available to every part of Canada; to the Pacific slope by a Peace River outlet, and east and west by the development of the St. Lawrence waterways, and we pledge ourselves to aid existing traffic channels and to increase port facilities on the great lakes, Hudson bay and the Atlantic and Pacific oceans, and to the establishment of a national highway system.
Incidentally in that declaration mention is made of a number of other transportation facilities, but specific mention is made of the Peace River outlet. So I think we may take it that there is no political conflict in a party sense, but that both party leaders have declared themselves as being in favour of the Peace River outlet. With the great need for the building of that road, with the preparations that have been made during the last eight years by the railway companies in their survey work, and in view of the fact that both political leaders have declared themselves in favour of building the road, why are we not busy building it? I imagine the only answer that will be given will be that this is a time when we ought to be practising economy rather than spending money. All governments in all countries of the world have a tendency to take that attitude. It has been the general practice, I think, of all governments, that in periods of depression governments, naturally reflecting the depressed feelings of the population and fearing popular criticism if they enter upon what would be regarded under such circumstances as extravagant expenditures, have refrained as much as possible from making expenditures during such periods and have practised rigid economy. Not only does that increase the depression by withdrawing credit from circulation, but by intensifying the psychological effects it makes the people generally more afraid of launching out into new enterprises, and thus adds greatly to the difficulties which depressions always bring.

I suggest on the contrary, that this is the psychological moment for the government of Canada to launch out into large expenditures. Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion) upon his remarks in connection with the report of the committee. I can associate myself with practically all his statements, with the possible exception of his reference to the outlet from the Peace River district to the Pacific.
To sum up briefly, I wish to place myself on record as being in accord with the statements made by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) concerning the Peace River outlet. In this connection the Minister of Railways said that it would be unfair to the people of Canada if at this time the government were to proceed with the construction, and for that reason he recorded his opposition. Although we have had surveys and re-surveys, examinations and re-examinations by engineers from the government and the various railways, he said that we were still in a position where in fairness to our people no definite decision could be made. Naturally Canadians want that route to be the most efficient possible of development. But I would also associate myself with the remarks of the previous speaker that the most important question before the people of Canada at this time is the question of unemployment. While it may be that in fairness to the people the route cannot be decided upon immediately, I say that in view of the economic situation and that the building of

this railway would give employment to from 10,000 to 20,000 men for some months to [DOT]come, it is doubly unfortunate that the government are not prepared to say "Go ahead at once."
As to the report itself, first of all I wish to commend the chairman of the committee, the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin), for his patience, his tact, and his fairness to every member of the committee. That the report is to all practical purposes a unanimous report is due almost entirely to his fairness and his tact.
Hear, hear.

The hon. member for
Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) in speaking to this report this afternoon, placed a good deal of valuable information before the people of Canada. I feel he is to be highly commended by the house and by the country for trying to bring home to us some realization of the colossal undertaking and of the enormous sums of money involved in the operating losses of the Canadian National Railways and its subsidiary companies. To my mind a great deal of the responsibility for the present position of the system rests with past governments. The picture which I have of the Canadian National Railways is that the Canadian people invested approximately $2,000,000,000 in the undertaking, and then they searched the world over and found the man they thought best fitted to handle it. But to my mind they did not take sufficient safeguards to ensure that the funds of Canada were spent to the best advantage.
Hear, hear.

I have no desire to criticize the officers of the Canadian National Railways. I say that any man placed in a responsible position where he has large sums of money to disburse, and is not given constructive criticism from time to time and vatched at all times, will invariably tend to jecome extravagant. So I say in the present case any remarks I have to make are not in criticism of the officers of the Canadian National Railways, but rather of the method adopted by the people of Canada for watching the operation of such a large undertaking.
The member for Stanstead thought that the appointment of directors, the setting up of the committee, and the report of the committee itself were all absolutely futile. I would say that this system of endeavouring to watch our large railway investment is not the best system. I have already stated so this evening. But I do say in justice to the committee that each and every member was conscientious,

serious and not politically partisan; all were conscientiously endeavouring to do something that they felt was necessary. That they have done something constructive I am quite satisfied, because if they have done nothing else they have brought to the attention of this house, of the board of directors, and of the officials of the system the necessity of doing something radical, and doing it at once.
In the report it will be noticed that as a result of the recommendation made by the president it is suggested that a commission should be established to investigate the whole railway situation in Canada. In that respect I would point out to hon. members that the total cost of the operation of both the Canadian National railway and the Canadian Pacific rialway must eventually be borne by the people of Canada; that every dollar spent in operation must eventually come from the pockets of the people. To my mind we have in both of these railway companies some of the most able men in their profession; they are men of knowledge and of vision; and if they would sit down across the table and not play railway politics, they would soon iron out some of the difficulties that are facing us at this time.
Hear, hear.

I do not think it is necessary to have a commission to investigate our railway troubles. I believe if the Prime Minister or the Minister of Railways in no uncertain terms notified the presidents of these two railway companies that we expect their cooperation for the elimination of so much futile competition-to use the words of my hon. friend from Stanstead-so much expensive competition, and that they must get down to business, the people of Canada would very soon see some light in the railway situation. That is something for which the government must take responsibility. I do not believe that a commission as suggested would get results, but I do believe that the government through the Prime Minister or the Minister of Railways can get results by simply insisting that those results shall be obtained.
It has been suggested that higher freight rates in the past would have prevented some of these losses; it has also been suggested that higher freight rates in the future would convert some of the present losses into profits. I would point out to hon. members that if we are to have higher freight rates we shall have a higher cost of producing wheat, lumber, and every other commodity. Transportation is a portion of the cost of producing everything, and to the extent that we in-

Railways and Shipping Report
crease freight rates we increase our cost of production. The problem in connection with increased freight rates is whether the individual producer is to absorb the increase or whether the country as a whole shall do sc.
In connection with the large deficit on the operation of the Canadian National Railways during the past year, I think it is only fair to call the attention of the house to the fact that during the past twelve months or more the management have retained on the pay roll numbers of men who in view of the economic depression would have been discharged had the railway company not been a nationally-owned system. To what extent their retention has prevented a reduction of the pay roll I could not say, but it would be an enormous sum. It has been suggested that there is not enough traffic in Canada to justify and make profitable the operation of both these railways. In this connection I would point out to the house that the greatest returns to the railway companies were in those years when the external trade of Canada was greatest. During the internal development of Canada it is only reasonable to assume that the deficits of the future will be even larger than those of the past.
Very few suggestions have been made as to what steps are necessary in order to remedy the losses we are suffering, but it is obvious that we require either greater revenue or a lower cost of operation. In order to bring about either of these results government policy is necessary, probably as expressed through the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways. There has been some discussion as to the constitution of the board of directors, as to the number of directors and as to the salaries they receive, and I think the arguments as to why the number of directors should not be reduced are logical. I would suggest for consideration that the Canadian National Railways might very well have a committee of the directors-not a committee of the management-numbering four, five or six, so located that they could meet often and for as long as it might be necessary, and that on this committee should be placed the responsibility for the operation of the road. They could then work in conjunction with the general board of directors as it is constituted at the present time. If we are to overcome the loss in the operation of this railway it is necessary that we should eliminate useless competition, and that we should do away with some of the services which the country can most easily do without. It may be that we will have to increase rates; it may be that we will have to
reduce the cost of operation; it may be that this reduction in the cost of operation will mean not only the reduction in salaries which was announced by the Minister of Railways this evening but that the government will have to go as far as to take responsibility for further reductions in the operating costs. That is something for government policy. It may be that the government will have to reorganize the capitalization of the company, and it may come to the point where the government will have to consider whether or not there are sufficient people in Canada at this time to make possible the profitable operation of the Canadian National Railways, and whether or not they will have to give consideration again to an immigration policy.
In connection with the committee, of which I had the honour to be a member, I feel quite justified in complimenting Sir Henry Thornton and the management of the company on the large mass of detailed information which they were able to give. I would suggest to the government, at the same time, that in constituting this committee another year they should endeavour to see that the committee is placed in possession of information as complete as possible, as early in the session as is possible. I do not know that any good purpose would have been served this year if we had been given more information at an earlier date, but it would have done no harm and might have done some good. I feel sure that the management and officials of the Canadian National Railways are fully seized of the importance of reducing every possible expenditure at this time, and I repeat that I believe the committee can take some credit to itself for having impressed upon the management the importance of this action being taken.
Just for a moment or two I should like to refer to that part of the report which deals with the Canadian government merchant marine. The original cost was approximately $80,000,000; the book value at present is about $45,000,000 and depreciation already set up amounts to about $17,000,000, so there is a present valuation of the steamers operated by the Canadian government merchant marine of approximately $28,000,000. That is the book value. We are told that the actual value is from $2,000,000 to $2,500,000, so the Canadian people have absorbed the loss of the entire original investment, plus the amounts it has been necessary to vote from year to year.

Privilege-Mr. Mackenzie King
Last year the operating loss was less than $600,000. The suggestion has been made by the committee that the government should give serious consideration to the disposal of these vessels, and with that recommendation I am in agreement, with one qualification. I suggest to the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) and to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) that the only justification for ever having had this service or for continuing it has been the development of the external trade of Canada. During the investigation we attempted to ascertain the value of the trade, both into and out of Canada, carried by those ships, but were unable to do so. I would suggest, therefore, that these ministers notify every board of trade in Canada and every user of these vessels that unless they can prove to the government that the people of Canada are justified in absorbing a loss of $600,000 a year, the service will be discontinued.
I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, that my time was so short, because there were several other remarks I should like to have made.
